items.body: Across its seventeen tracks, Wahj brings together electronics, industrial textures, processed strings, Arabic vocal traditions and fractured rhythms in combinations that keep changing shape. Individual elements remain recognisable without settling into familiar forms, while images of voice, disappearance, radiance and return recur throughout the album. Wahj took shape over five years, and the events of that period inevitably entered the music. As Toni Geitani explains in the accompanying interview, the album was not initially conceived as a meditation on collapse. The idea emerged gradually as the circumstances surrounding its composition changed. Collapse here is not a single catastrophic moment. Ruin exists alongside what persists, with Geitani attentive to the lives and voices that political violence can obscure. This runs through the lyrics as well as the music. Voices appear and disappear, sometimes sounding like invocations, sometimes carrying fragments of collective memory. On the brief “Sawtuka”, Geitani repeats, “Raise your voice higher and higher. Even if they bind you, even if they take you through death, the echo of your voice will remain forever.” The refrain turns persistence itself into an act of resistance. “2092” projects the idea into an imagined future in which “every fascist has fallen, and their glory belongs to nothingness,” before asking, “Does love remain when everything has vanished?” “Hal”, “Ruwaydan Ruwaydan” and the extended instrumental closer “Madda Mudadda” draw on ritual, repetition and moments of ecstatic release, with their meanings left open. The title, Wahj, points towards radiance, although Geitani gives the word no easy redemptive meaning. Light appears amid destruction, sometimes faintly, and does not cancel what surrounds it. In “Tuyoor”, the image is carried by birds: “The birds flying above you do not belong to the ruler who oppressed you. They watch the sky, not the earth beneath you.” The image opens a space outside the authority of the ruler, even while that authority continues to shape life below. Throughout Wahj, Geitani keeps returning to such spaces: voices that outlast attempts to silence them, traces of love after disappearance, and forms of life that continue amid devastation. To discuss the making of Wahj, we approched Toni Geitani directly. Wahj is described as an album about collapse, but one that refuses to remain trapped within its concept. Across the record, images of ruin, mourning, exile, and disappearance are constantly accompanied by gestures toward radiance, return, and endurance. How did you approach balancing these opposing forces while writing the album? I didn’t start working on the album with any intention of a “theme”, in this case collapse. I also wasn’t trying to narrow down the album to one thematic focus. It was an intuitive process that mostly guided the work. But it is true that as the project developed over five years, a lot of horrific events unfolded; consecutively and sometimes simultaneously. This naturally affected the relation to my work in a way that pushed me into ending up with these tracks, which I could eventually describe as being about collapse. By saying that the album refuses to be reduced to collapse, I’m intentionally pushing back against the idea that collapse is only a sudden, singular catastrophe. I was born in the 1990s in post-civil-war Lebanon, so from early on I was surrounded by war stories told by family and friends. After continuous exposure to these stories throughout my life, I came to understand that they were not stories of the past only, but of a collapse that kept resurfacing in different forms. At the same time, however, I was also exposed to another image of collapse that dominated global media and felt especially present in my teens in the 2000s. It was that of an image imported from the West, romanticized, and flattened into spectacle. It also ignores how, for some populations, collapse is already ongoing rather than a problem of the future or an isolated incident that can be inherited and prolonged. That difference matters to me because, for many of us, imperialism, colonialism, and capitalism are not warnings of an apocalypse to come, but they morph to become ongoing and almost fixed conditions. So when I was writing Wahj, I didn’t feel that I was trying to balance opposing forces simply because I do not see them as opposing, but inevitably coexisting. Instead, I was trying to remain faithful to everything catastrophe-centered narratives tend to erase: memory, resistance, regeneration, and the human capacity to continue. They are what must be reclaimed from within it. The lyrics repeatedly return to voices, echoes, and acts of calling out across distance. In “Sawtuka” (“Your Voice”), for example, the refrain insists that a voice survives even imprisonment or death, while tracks like “2092” and “Tuyoor” are structured around questions of who is listening and who remains absent. What role does the voice play in Wahj—as memory, resistance, testimony, or something else entirely? For this album, I composed the music before writing the lyrics. I would often record a vocal melody, sometimes with words that made sense and sometimes not, simply to find a fitting flow and have it as a placeholder until the final vocal recording. But before I began writing and recording the lyrics, the genocide in Gaza began alongside the war on Lebanon in 2023, so I stopped working on the album because I felt uneasy about prioritizing it. At that point, nothing made sense anymore. But somehow, by the beginning of 2025, I found the motivation to finish the project, and thus the lyrics were written. In my opinion, the voice can hold many roles at once, including the ones mentioned in the question. It is not intended to be a tool for meaning-making, but rather a presence moving through space, carrying the emotional and political conditions of that space with it. However, its position is immanent rather than observational. It does not stand outside the world to explain it. Instead, it emerges from within that world and continually reaches outward, while refusing to die. The lyrics inevitably reflect the experience of witnessing a 24/7 livestreamed ongoing Palestinian genocide, and the rage, injustice, betrayal, pain, and constant aggression we have been dealing with for many years. However, I do not wish to limit the album’s interpretation to the events of the past three years. As I mentioned earlier, collapse is not a one-time event or a singular fall, but I insist that it emerges from an ongoing oppression imposed on us by the same death machine. Musically, the album moves between processed classical instruments, layālī-inspired vocal passages, industrial textures, dark ambient atmospheres, and fractured electronic rhythms without ever fully settling into any one genre. Did you begin with a clear sonic vision for Wahj, or did this hybrid language emerge gradually during the five years of recording between 2021 and 2025? I did begin with a fairly clear sonic vision for Wahj, in the sense that from the beginning I wanted it to explore different genres and subgenres while still remaining rooted in electronics. What emerged gradually was not that intention itself, but the specific language the album took on through time, collaboration, experimentation, and everything that happened across those years. After releasing my first album in 2018, I wanted to keep exploring and collaborating before putting out another record. Between 2018 and 2020, I performed many live shows in Lebanon, where improvisation became an important space for testing new ideas and compositions. Over time, this left me with more than a hundred sketches, from which I selected the ones that felt less attached to a single genre and more committed to a shared atmosphere and universe, even if that universe itself remains unstable and fluctuating. When I began my studies at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam in 2021, that process expanded further. Being surrounded by many different kinds of musicians pushed me to explore classical instrumentation, processing, and different digital approaches in ways I had not tried beforehand. I recorded many phrases and ideas with musicians there, often without knowing exactly what their final form would be, because part of the process was discovering how their playing could be transformed and absorbed into the album’s sonic world. In that sense, the hybrid language of the record was both intended and gradually revealed. As mentioned earlier, I returned to working on the album in the beginning of 2025, and that final period inevitably shaped the work in a profound way. So while the album’s sonic foundation was there from the beginning, its final form was shaped by a long process of experimentation, disruption, and response to the world it was being made within. Several tracks evoke futures rather than simply documenting the present. The title “2092,” in particular, imagines a distant horizon where “every fascist has fallen and their glory belongs to nothingness,” while love and memory continue to endure. What attracted you to speculative or future-oriented thinking as a way of responding to contemporary political realities? I would like to make a distinction between futurism as typically understood through a Eurocentric lens which is rooted in Euro-American frameworks and historically entangled with imperialism and fascism – and counterfuturism that emerged from the Global South which functions to complicate normalized notions of time and technology rather than projecting a single vision of the future. And this is precisely what I intend to convey in the practice of imagining futures in the album, which attempt to articulate a cultural politics of time and become a means of writing alternative histories that distance themselves from any established history already written. This could mean reclaiming the right to think beyond imperialist scripts through collective knowledge, agency, and world-making rather than celebrating rupture, domination, or heroic modernity. In other words, I’m trying to open possibilities from within collapse, and thus, this framework differs from futurism as an approach for technocratic future-thinking. For example in “2092”, I try to treat the future as a tool to ask whose futures have been denied or flattened, instead of assuming it operates in a single path of progress. The political visions I sing about are not predictions, but they gesture toward an intense need to imagine the aftermath of collapse in the hope that something promising might emerge from it. That being said, I don’t intend for my songs to be frontal or overly obvious in their interpretation, and I welcome listeners to bring different meanings to them. You wrote a master’s thesis titled Sampling as a Political Medium, examining questions of power, appropriation, and cultural memory. Wahj incorporates repurposed regional sounds and references while constructing an entirely new sonic language. How has your thinking about sampling evolved since that research, and how do those ideas inform the album’s relationship to Arabic musical traditions and collective memory? My thinking on sampling has certainly evolved, although I do not see it as a linear progression that concluded with my thesis. The research was conducted alongside the creation of the album and I continue to work with samples, therefore I am always interacting with this topic. Throughout Wahj, I work with both political and non-political samples that either have a political or non-political intention. For example, samples from my personal life, my urban surroundings, and of traditional instruments, the choice is more nuanced because it’s integrated and processed within the soundscape and ambient textures. However, for samples that are more frontal and forward, like the sampling of Amal Dunqul’s poem, “Spartacus’ Last Words” in “Madda Mudadda” the intention is more clearly deliberate and explicit. These choices are bound to spill into collective memory, as I am borrowing sounds from my surroundings and heritage. Take the sample of Lebanese singers Sabah, Wadih El Safi, and Walid Gholmieh in “Wasla”; I was drawn to their voices for reasons I can’t quite articulate. But the moment I tried fitting the sample into the track, it felt seamless. My sampling choices are meant to re-activate archive sound, and insert these historical moments into the present to let them speak again through a different context. All voice samples from the album come from televised interviews, and I chose them not only for their raw, untampered sound, but also because they carry something of the world they were recorded in. To sample them is to pull them back into light and reactivate voices forced to be erased for new audiences, while also making visible the power structures that determine whose memory is preserved and who is erased from the record. Ultimately, these sampling choices are always, in some way, in conversation with the cultural memory I carry, bringing the historical in contact with the contemporary. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Toni Geitani历时五年完成，将电子、工业质感、处理化弦乐、阿拉伯人声传统与碎裂节奏交织于十七首曲目之中，元素不断变形重组，兼具可识别性与陌生感。专辑并非预先设定主题，而是在创作过程中逐渐成为对崩塌的沉思——不是单一灾难时刻，而是废墟与存续并存的状态，暴力政治往往遮蔽的生命与声音成为关注焦点。人声在专辑中时而召唤、时而携带集体记忆碎片，歌词将坚持本身转化为抵抗行为，并以仪式、重复与迷狂释放构建开放意义的瞬间。专辑标题指向光辉却不赋予廉价救赎意义，光明在毁灭中微弱浮现而不取消周围的存在。整张作品在艺术原创性、跨文化融合与思想深度上均展现出强烈个人视角，是实验电子与世界音乐交汇地带中值得关注的声音实践。

items.body: Pendulum is a singular piano trio featuring French pianist Benoît Delbecq with Danish double bass player Jonas Westergaard and drummer Peter Bruun (both Westergaard and Bruun have collaborated before with fellow Danish pianist Søren Kjærgaard). Bruun initiated this trio in 2024 as part of his ambitious research project exploring new approaches to musical time (Multitemporal movement and embodiment through Rhythmic Design at The Danish National Academy of Music). The Pendulum trio investigates all aspects of this classic format, including the most basic sensibilities of space and time, avoiding rigid structures, allowing instead for balance, elegance and fluidity. It challenges us to listen to its music as resonant arcs or shared fields of presence rather than defined by linear time, and explores new ways to transform free improvisation gravity into groove. Delbeq suggested that the trio will play with the presence of physical pendulums on stage, symbolizing the elasticity of time and giving a sense of pulse. These oscillating bodies guide the subtle, cyclical shifts in the music, which, paradoxically, feels familiar: music that sways and breathes, while finding rhythm in the inevitability of motion. The trio releases its eight-volume EP series, Arcs , nearly three hours of music, in a monthly release cycle that began in May and will conclude in December 2026. These Arcs offer Pendulum’s idiosyncratic, enigmatic, lyrical universe, in which metric relations, shifting balances, and elastic phrasing are woven together in a kaleidoscopic manner. Each volume swings on its own terms, with no intention to offer a linear narrative, and uses distinct compositional fragments, notated and graphic scores. But the whole project accumulates into an open body of work that allows us to feel how time bends, breathes, and searches for an elusive balance. The Pendulum trio invites listeners to form their own path through the eight volumes and discover different insights and relations in their own time. Arc No. 1 Pendulum describes this volume: “Time leans before it moves. Motion unfolds patiently, stretching and rebounding with quiet elasticity. What propels the arc is not force but attentiveness, which allows duration to bend and return without breaking. Each swing carries clarity and restraint, revealing time as something more shaped than measured”. The trio suggests sparse, deep listening, labyrinthine architectures with patient and subtle, cyclical-rhythmic shifts, best captured in the aptly titled, 17-minute minimalist “Exercice Elastique”, that patiently gravitates into a most delicate, vulnerable, quite irreverent groove. Arc No. 2 “Afterwards appears before it is recognized. Movement writes itself into space, leaving subtle traces that guide listening rather than direction. Rhythms form paths, both adaptable and responsive, where perception stretches between memory and anticipation. The arc remains fluid, shaped by change rather than arrival”. Pendulum sketches an almost abstract, empty map, from which it begins to imagine possible contours and paths, and how to find its inner, spatial logic, and its subtle rhythmic shifts, finally realized on “Plasticity”. Arc No. 3 “Movement turns inward. Each gesture is weighted, deliberate, and reduced to necessity. Time thickens as motion slows, inviting attention to settle inside the smallest shifts. The arc transforms discreetly, as intensity is held beneath restraint. Balance is discovered through presence, not display”. The 31-minute “Buto” corresponds with the hyper-slow and hyper-controlled motion of the Japanese avant-dance theatre, Butō (舞踏), that resists and fixated conception of time. Pendulum’s fragile balance was realized through an austere, cryptic, and often almost silent presence that keeps triggering our imagination, and not by technical display or mastery. Arc No. 4 “Wooden time moves with grain and resistance. Motion creaks, sways, and negotiates its own structure. Oscillation becomes tactile, shaped by friction and patience. The arc holds multiple possibilities at once, allowing form and freedom to coexist without resolution. The rings of time are both counted and counting”. The trio focuses on its essence, the ever-negotiated arcs that blur the distinction between form and freedom, and question our conception of linear time, turning it into a spiritual riddle, a kōan. Arc No. 5 “A phase shifts nearly unnoticed. Motion lightens, stepping carefully through softened contours. Layers thin and overlap, revealing phrasing where gestures begin and fade. The arc listens closely to its own balance, finding meaning in nuance rather than emphasis. The push and pull are their own reason for being”. Pendulum refines its fragile, nuanced equilibrium with melodic threads that patiently, hesitantly flirt with familiar, playful, and resonant piano trio dynamics. Arc No. 6 (to be released on October 10) “Momenta accumulate through return. Motion becomes practiced, framed by shared gravity and memory. Energy circulates without urgency, shaped by repetition and transformation. The past is present and future at once”. A further, urgent, cyclical rhythmic refinement is offered, faithfully captured in the short pieces “Arc” and “Dance”, shaped by nuanced repetitions and transformations. Arc No. 7 (to be released on November 9) “Time folds into itself. Multiple cycles coexist, asymmetrical yet connected. Movement breathes across layered durations, allowing contradiction to remain unresolved. The arc sustains density without weight, continuity without uniformity. Listening is wide enough to hold all the all of it”. Pendulum’s music plays a touch-and-go game in its own fragmented musical continuum, sustaining density without weight, continuity without uniformity, but with more structural focus. Arc No. 8 (to be released on December 9) “Strange tools reveal their logic through use. Motion disperses, leaving resonance rather than momentum. What remains feels everywhere at once, absorbed into space and attention. The arc settles without closing, as stillness carries the last trace of movement forward. It is the beginning of the end and the end of the beginning”. The concluding volume is not an end to this fascinating journey but a sort of beginning. The Pendulum trio already inhabited its own elastic conception of time, as the devoted listeners to this journey, and has established its idiosyncratic language. But Pendulum’s music tells us something deeper about life and the inevitable changes we experience throughout life. This trio asks us to adapt our time sensibility to its subtle transformations, fully embrace and be deeply attuned to our own ubiquitous cyclical and oscillating arcs, as we move forward, attempting to maintain an elusive balance. <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-1">Opening Arcs: Arc No. 1 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-2">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 2 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-3">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 3 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-4">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 4 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-5">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 5 by ILK</a > Email This BlogThis! items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是法国钢琴家Benoît Delbecq与丹麦低音提琴手Jonas Westergaard、鼓手Peter Bruun组成的钢琴三重奏项目Pendulum的系列EP合集。鼓手Bruun于2024年发起这一项目，作为其在丹麦皇家音乐学院多节奏运动研究计划的一部分，探讨钢琴三重奏这一经典编制在时间与空间感知上的全新可能。音乐刻意回避刚性结构，追求平衡、优雅与流动性，将自由即兴的重力转化为律动。现场演奏时使用实体钟摆象征时间的弹性。整套Arcs系列以月度发布形式呈现，包含八卷近三小时的音乐，采用记谱与图形谱结合的作曲片段，以回旋式节奏位移与弹性乐句编织成多层次的声音宇宙。作品强调深度聆听、循环结构与时间的延展，而非线性叙事，邀请听众按自己的节奏在八卷中构建聆听路径。

items.body: When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. A form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes Wind Paths by Philippe Deschamps   The cover already offers a statement of intent. A shifting blue, crossed by pale brushstrokes, occupies the entire field, leaving a small white mark near the lower edge. It could be water observed at close range, air made visible, a photograph taken in motion during a crossing. The image refuses to settle. Wind Paths follows the same impulse, entrusting its identity to whatever passes, bends and changes density. Philippe Deschamps gathers wind, waves and rain into music that is brief and lucid, animated by a calm that retains its sense of movement. Four pieces and just over ten minutes form a single current. The compact running time keeps every element clear of decorative contemplation. The chords move slowly, changing color by small degrees; the guitar disperses its outlines; the synthesizers hold open an even light, gently varied from within. The field recordings enter the wider fabric discreetly. Sea and rain shed their role as illustrative background and become pressure, an irregular pulse, a measure beyond human intention. The record listens to the landscape as it transforms it. The new gesture lies in the voice. Deschamps trained as a Baroque countertenor and draws on that experience here, freeing it from text. The vocal tones stretch, overlap and take on the quality of warm currents. No phrase reaches for​ meaning. The body emerges through breath, then merges with guitar and recorded air. This fusion forms the emotional centre of the EP. It offers a fragile presence. The listener recognises a human figure and immediately watches it dissolve into the broader movement. It is a simple decision on paper, decisive in its effect. Deschamps’ path has been leading towards this synthesis for some time. Introduced to the piano as a child, later a singer, bassist and guitarist in rock and post rock groups, then trained in film sound at La Fémis, the French composer has developed an ambient body of work since 2022, nourished by natural phenomena and mental images. “Blue Baths,” “Forest of my Nights,” “The Silence of Pallas,” “Remember the Clouds,” “Endless Vanishing Lines,” and “Entering the Ocean” mark the stages of a coherent inquiry. Ocean, sky, darkness and distance provide a different organizing principle each time. Wind Paths distils that inquiry even further. The voice enters the frame and alters the relationship between landscape and memory. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration :: His experience in cinema emerges through the precision of each entrance and fade. Deschamps understands the weight of a sound placed an instant earlier or later, and knows how to let a detail acquire prominence without demanding it. Here, that sensitivity produces a fluid montage. Forms follow one another through affinity, carried by a slow pulse that resembles breathing and, at times, the movement of the tide. There are no spectacular peaks, refrains or turns designed to reclaim the listener’s attention. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration. At certain points, a low line supports the entire field; elsewhere, the texture grows lighter and the voice seems to arrive from an immeasurable distance. Few materials, carefully chosen. The record’s ambient purity grows from this economy. Its sound world possesses body and depth, and maintains an almost tactile transparency. Silence appears within the gaps and along the fading edges of notes. Even the fuller passages leave an open area where the wind around the listener, distant traffic or movement elsewhere in the house can still be heard. The music welcomes such intrusions. Its open character encourages a porous relationship with the present. Wind Paths can drift at low volume and preserve its identity; under closer listening, it reveals subtle changes, harmonies slipping sideways and voices layered with restraint. Such control brings its own risk. At times, the music’s gentleness brushes against a beauty held too safely, polished until friction and surprise have almost disappeared. Its brevity sharpens the issue: certain openings withdraw just as they acquire an unexpected inflection. The ending arrives early and leaves a desire for one further stretch, perhaps a little less serene. This limitation also clarifies the nature of the project. Wind Paths chooses a form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes. It asks for attention without insisting upon it. The title speaks of invisible paths, and the music realizes that idea with remarkable coherence. Each element follows its own direction, guided by shared currents. The voice rises, the guitar fades, the harmonies change their angle. Deschamps has created one of his most lucid works, bringing together his vocal training, cinematic sensibility and ambient practice within a form that feels accessible, intimate and precise. When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. Wind Paths is available on Silent Sonic. [Bandcamp] Wind Paths by Philippe DeschampsThe post Philippe Deschamps :: Wind Paths (Silent Sonic) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: Philippe Deschamps 的 EP《Wind Paths》仅十分钟出头，以四首短曲构成一个连贯的气流。专辑融合田野录音（海浪、雨声）与合成器缓慢展开的和声层次，吉他轮廓被刻意消解，留出均匀的光。核心突破在于 Deschamps 将其巴洛克假声男高音训练引入环境音乐——人声脱离文本，成为温暖气流，与乐器和自然录音融为一体又随即消散，形成脆弱却决定性的人类在场感。这张作品延续了他自 2022 年以来以海洋、天空、黑暗、距离为线索的创作脉络，将电影声音设计经验注入极简环境结构中，以微小变化积累张力，最终蒸馏出风景与记忆之间新的关系。

items.body: Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure Materia by GIULIO ALDINUCCI   At first there is weight. A quiet, almost geological pressure that arrives before recognition, touching the body before it reaches the mind. Materia begins in that dark place. Sound has volume, temperature, even something resembling a will of its own. It advances slowly and alters the scale of things, like a sudden bank of fog moving in. Sight loses its authority and the ear becomes a larger organ. Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. The composer, born in Siena, Tuscany, reaches this point after years devoted to landscape, memory and the voice stripped of semantic meaning. The experience developed under the name Obsil and the chapter that began with Tarsia have shaped a coherent body of work, nourished by field recordings, choral presences and electronic transformations. Borders And Ruins examined the nature of territory; Disappearing In A Mirror and Shards Of Distant Times shifted the tension towards identity and memory; Real sought a personal reality within the excess of digital mediation. Materia, Aldinucci’s fifth album for Karlrecords, condenses that history into an essential gesture: taking a tightly packed mass of sound, carving into it, paring it back and searching for what is already alive​ inside. The album was released on September 18, 2026. Here accumulation and subtraction become emotional acts. Aldinucci gathers frequencies as scattered memories might be gathered after years apart, then removes the excess and listens into the space left behind by what has disappeared. Time, too, acquires substance. It is broken into minute units and reassembled according to an order that escapes the familiar pulse. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure, through inner tides, through the way a distant voice rises from the haze and immediately loses its face. These are slow movements filled with secret life. Their apparent stillness is alive with motion. The six pieces form a single body lasting just under 43 minutes. Density remains the active principle, capable of changing state while retaining its gravity. The depths below sustain the journey with a telluric continuity. Above them appear distorted choirs, echoes, drifting particles and sounds that preserve a human trace after language and origin have fallen away. The titles sketch a constellation of absence: “Not Here,” the shadow cast by noise, ash and distant waves, the absolute finality of “Never,” evening, then light caught in a dream. The music receives these images and preserves their indeterminacy. Each one works within the act of listening, removed from plot and close to the freedom of involuntary association. “Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time.” ~Mirco Salvadori The voice is central. It rises like a collective memory without face or biography, suspended between comfort and alarm. At times it resembles someone calling across an immense distance; elsewhere it takes on the substance of a thought formed in the body before words. Aldinucci understands the power of vocal fragments and frees them from any narrative duty. What remains is breath, impulse, a tremor that reminds the listener of human fragility. Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time. “Come Luce, In Sogno,” chosen as the advance single, offers a discreet way into the album. The light invoked by its title contains dust and density. It filters through opaque layers and produces figures already moving towards dissolution. Dreaming becomes a mode of knowledge. A detail can expand until it fills the entire field of perception, while an enormous event contracts into a brief vibration. This instability runs through the whole work. Time seems to lengthen; then an almost imperceptible shift alters the landscape. Sound retains warmth and a question that has yet to find words. The cover helps reveal the character of the work. A white façade multiplies concave modules, dark openings and curves that look identical only at a glance. The eye finds order, then differences, shadows, stains and minor signs of wear. It is a serial form made vulnerable by time and by the material from which it is built. Aldinucci’s music behaves in much the same way. It turns repetition into change, raises immense structures and allows irregularity to bring them alive. Each surface hints at another depth. No answer comes. The desire to look again grows stronger. The concentration of the sound demands complete attention. A moment’s distraction can break the spell, and some passages deliberately court saturation. This is an exacting choice. Materia requires time, an appropriate volume and a measure of solitude. In return it offers a rare experience, moving listening beyond taste and into consciousness. Its forms entrust their appeal to a slower force, like the memory of a place never visited. There is familiarity and a faint fear. The unknown takes on an intimate temperature. “Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought.” ~Mirco Salvadori Throughout Aldinucci’s career, recording the world has carried the value of a living archive. A landscape could hold a story; a procession could deliver into the present voices already receding into the distance; an ordinary noise could open a passage through perception. Materia brings this practice close to an elemental dimension. Here substance comes before place and contact before narrative. Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought. This is where its power lies. The album speaks of the human condition through feeling. The need to give chaos a shape meets the fascination of whatever resists a final form. Every cut removes part of the original mass; subtraction reveals an unforeseen outline. The music breathes between these impulses, tightens, withdraws and fills out again. At times it seems about to disclose something. Then that something changes substance and becomes pure listening. Materia is expansive, gathered into a fierce intensity and charged with physical mystery. Giulio Aldinucci reaches one of the most mature expressions of his artistic language and gives contemporary ambient music an album with moral as well as sonic weight. When the final vibration ends, silence feels altered, thicker, almost conscious. Within that silence passes an intuition that cannot quite be held: perhaps the human spirit is precisely this restless substance, seeking form while knowing that every form is temporary. For just under 43 minutes, Materia gives it a body and lets it sing. Materia is available on Karlrecords. items._cn_summary: 意大利作曲家Giulio Aldinucci的第五张专辑《Materia》以六首曲目共43分钟的篇幅，探索声音的物质性与心理空间。专辑以准地质般的低频压力开场，将田野录音、变形人声合唱与电子处理融为一体，通过加法与减法的交替手法，将密集的声响团块雕琢剥离，露出内部的存留物。节奏不以脉冲呈现，而是以压力变化、内在潮汐和远处人声的若隐若现来传递。曲目标题如《Not Here》《Never》等勾勒出缺席的星座，暗示语言与起源消逝后仍保存人性痕迹的回响。整体呈现出一种缓慢、隐秘、充满内省张力的氛围架构，将记忆、领土与身份的主题压缩为对声音密度的持续冥想。

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 512, Slovenian improvising pianist and bandleader Kaja Draksler creates an exclusive Wire mix Kaja Draksler studied jazz at a music-oriented high school in Ljubljana, later enrolling at the Conservatory of Amsterdam. There, her instructor, the British composer Richard Ayres, asked her the simple question,“What do you want to do?”, which set her on a path that would chafe against the jazz orthodoxy. In August Punkt.Vrt. Plastik, her long-running trio with Swedish bassist Petter Eldh and German drummer Christian Lillinger, released their fourth album, Kompress, while another of her groups, matter 100, releases its debut True Or False this October. This exclusive mix, she explains, is “more of a collage, where I mostly take excerpts from different pieces, placing them one after the other, and, at times, one of top of the other. The track selection is a mix of my own music and music I love, with a bit of a focus on piano and voices.” Tracklist Kaja Draksler “Prst, roka, laket” (excerpt) Vaqif Mustafazadə “Bizim Bakı Gecələri” (excerpt) Luciano Berio “A La Femminisca” Christian Lillinger “Poliform” (excerpt) Punkt.Vrt.Plastik “EKV” Vince Staples “Get Paid” New London Chamber Choir & James Wood “Serment” (excerpt) Georges Aperghis “Recitation 10_ left part, 1st version” Nina Simone “Who Am I” Irena Z Tomažin “Rain” (excerpt) Pauline Oliveros “Horse Sings From A Cloud” (excerpt) J Gallus “Mirabile Misterium: De Nativitate Circumcisione Et Epiphania Domini Huelgas Ensemble” matter 100 “Rushing Through The Night” (excerpt) Czajka & Puchacz “Wacky Compass” (excerpt(s)) MIA “Sunshowers” (excerpt) Cecil Taylor “Pt 4 Glossalalia” (excerpt) Craig Taborn “Glossolalia” Kaja Draksler Octet “Come See” (excerpt) Andrew Parrot “De Torrente” Judith Berkson “Castle” Ellen Arkbro “For Organ And Brass” (excerpt) matter 100 “Alternating Current” Read Peter Margasak’s full interview with Kaja Draksler in The Wire 512. Pick up a copy in our online shop. Subscribers can read the full article in the digital archive here.

items._cn_summary: 斯洛文尼亚即兴钢琴家Kaja Draksler为The Wire杂志制作的独家混音作品，呈现出拼贴式的选曲结构。曲目涵盖她本人的作品、爵士经典、当代古典以及多元文化的声音片段，包括Luciano Berio的人声实验、Pauline Oliveros的深度聆听理念作品、Cecil Taylor的自由即兴，以及阿塞拜疆传统音乐元素。Draksler在混音中将不同来源的片段并置叠加，而非简单的曲目串联，形成层次交错的聆听体验。选曲聚焦钢琴与人声主题，融合自由爵士、前卫古典与世界音乐元素，展现出即兴音乐人对声音材料组织方式的独特思考。整体呈现出策展式的艺术视野，混合个人创作与所推崇的音乐，揭示其美学谱系的多元来源。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An unusual yet fully-progressive undertaking of setting literary stories to music using jazz-fusion artists.1. "The Sinking Spell" (4:40) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice enters with some effect applied while the four musicians, Steve Swallow, Jack DeJohnette, Carla Bley, and Terje Rypdal apply their talents to constructing a loose and reactive soundtrack to Robert's rendering of this Edward Gorey story. Terje is particularly flamboyant (almost in a Steve Hackett way!) while Carla, Steve, and Jack are pretty dynamic in their own right. Perhaps Robert's best, most unique performance on the album and maybe the best collective Jazz-Rock Fusionary exposition as well. (9.125/10) 2. "The Object Lesson" (5:00) piano, bass and swelling cymbal crashes back Robert's rather flat/monotone delivery of this story. Eventually the musicians fall into a kind of groove with Jack DeJohnette's rock drumming and Terje Rypdal and Carla Bley's Canterbury organ saw-like expressions. The music is not great, not fully-formed or composed for much other than dramatic support, but it works (it's better than the story being told). (8.75/10)3 "The Insect God" (5:00) some truly top-notch Jazz-Rock Fusion is used to present another sobering and not-for-children's-ears story. The music quartet of Bley, Rypdal, Swallow, and drummer Jack DeJohnette are all on the same page of aggressive and insistent delivery while Robert and spoken-word "backing vocalists" render their fast-talking approach to dramatic story-telling. (8.75/10)4 "The Doubful Guest" (4:45) finally! some thoroughly-composed music! It's a challenging weave of off-timed hi-speed drum and keyboard music in which Steve and Terje contribute long-held, pensive notes on their respective instruments. All the while Robert delivers a near-spoken word story with a little more flair and enthusiasm than the past two. The overall weave really works--has no glaring flaws or inconsistencies. I like the way the musical performances ramp up toward the end: especially Terje's guitar shredding and Carla's breadth of synth strings chords. (9.125/10)5 "The Remembered Visit" (6:25) voice with syncopated bass and synth-strings pulses, adding piano and Mellotron "ooo"s and "aaah"s, then treated electric guitar notes and some background drumming. In the third minute the drums and bass play get more animated--still orchestral and reactive, though, more than "song" oriented. Where Robert's delivery starts out dramatic and engaged, it begins to sound a bit like rote reading in places. But then things slow down for the background vocal-supported passage in the fifth minute--which has the effect of seeming to bring Robert back into the spirit of the story. From there out he feels fully-present in his story-telling. Effective. (8.875/10)6 "The Hapless Child" (7:00) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice and vocal/story-telling stylings are here backed by music that feels more like theater music: it's incidental and yet has a personality all its own--as if taking on the characteristics of Robert's story's characters. Nothing is flowing or timed, almost all of it feels impressionistic and reactive more than composed and prescribed. There is one theme that feels prepared: the whole-band motif that starts at 2:58 when Robert starts singing about the start of Charlotte Sophia's boarding school experience, but at 4:20 everything devolves to simple piano--just before launching into a more dynamic and drum-and-guitar-driven theme. What a horrifying Dickensian tale! Carla Bley's odd chord choices hold the whole thing down but it's Steve Swallow's obtuse bass notes and Terje Rypdal's sharp, stinging guitar notes that bring forth and amplify the Poe-like atmosphere of the story. Wow! What an experience! Definitely not your typical bed-time story! Even children's theatre would be scarred and marred for decades if they brought children in to hear this one! Still, it is a rather powerful and effective delivery mechanism. (13.25/15)Total Time:I have to admit that I was not prepared for either the album's total dedication to story telling nor it's dark and rather dismal, even desolate, Dickensian/Brothers Grimm/Edgar Allen Poe story lines. While I love the literate nature of the stories, I'm a bit disturbed by their unsettling subject matters. At the same time, I appreciate these adventurous musicians for their commitment to the expansion of that which music and Jazz-Rock Fusion can do. B/four stars; though admirable to take on such an odd and ambitious undertaking, I feel that the stories and music do not always match as well as the artists/producers may have wanted. Nor are the instrumental performances and song/soundtrack compositions as polished and coordinated as well as one might expect or desire from this stellar line-up.

items.body: With Hor-Cheret, we welcome a new project presented as a collaboration between members of Vortex, Nam-Khar, and Delta Komplex, complemented by a few more artists. The project’s name alludes to Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. With an album title referring to an ancient nomadic law of hospitality, Hor-Cheret offers an intriguing metaphor and, in my view, a critical perspective on today’s world. It certainly offers food for thought, but above all, this is music to be discovered. From the very first notes, a distinct Ritual influence emerges through the percussion and the use of traditional acoustic instruments. While the percussion reinforces the album’s ritualistic character, the listener gradually discovers a dark atmosphere shaped by deep sound waves. Elements of Dark-Ambient and Industrial music are clearly present. An Ethereal female voice occasionally takes on a narrative role while simultaneously enhancing the sense of mysticism. The male voice also serves a narrative function, while some of the lyrics possess a distinctly poetic quality. This is a superbly crafted album in a genre that suffers from a lack of quality projects and inconsistent production standards. Hor-Cheret’s debut is a release to be savored and cherished. (Rating:8½). Listen to “In The Shadow Ov Power”: In The Shadow Ov Power by HOR-CHERET About Hor-Cheret Hor-Cheret is a new collaborative project pairing members of Vortex, Nam-Khar and Delta Komplex with additional contributors, presented on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Its name references Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. Nam-Khar is the ritual ambient project of Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009, previously paired with Vortex on “Nag-Hammadi” in 2022 and “The Sarajevo Spiral” in 2024. Delta Komplex is a German electronic band founded in 2019 around Minu-Schirin Samimi and Tufana, known for the 2022 album “Veils”. “Nanawatai”, Hor-Cheret’s debut album, was released on 7 November 2025 in a limited handnumbered digipak edition.

items.body: I recently wrote about an innovation currently taking place in noise rock, where noise rock bands that have embraced everything from more elaborate and thoughtful songwriting to unsettling electronic experimentation on their 2026 releases. Some that I didn’t mention have taken on a spacious, extended approach to the genre while others have embraced a dense, radical brevity. Bands across the genre have been stretching and morphing the style into previously unknown forms over the last few years, but it feels like this year has been especially fruitful in this regard. Tankerlow’s sophomore effort Slagroom can safely be added to the growing list of innovative noise rock that has been released this year, and it stands among the best.On Slagroom, Tankerlow employs a variety of sonic and dynamic approaches. Several tracks slowly unfold with a drone-like quality. There is an openness to those tracks that allows them to breathe and bloom on their own without being forced into a preconceived form by the composers. This natural pacing gives the impression that the members of Tankerlow exhibited considerable restraint, especially within a genre known for its compositional density. This restraint is most prominent toward the end of “Ergo/Ogre” when the song gets so quiet that the listener can hear the buzz of the amp underneath vocalist Guy Azulay’s unsettling, quiet moans. Yet, within that restraint is an impressive, free-wheeling aptitude for experimentation. That experimentation is prominent throughout the album, and not just with the more expansive tracks. Hammered dulcimers, pitched-down looped vocals that sound like a horn, and feedback accidentally created in the studio are all features on the groove-oriented “Formula Baby.” This combination of various compositional approaches and experimentation give each track their own character, a trait that is sadly hard to find in noise rock.What is at least partially responsible for that experimentation is the fact that the band spent over “two consistent and meticulous years in the studio,” which also explains the high quality of Slagroom’s production. Slagroom is, simply put, the best-sounding noise rock I’ve heard all year. Aspects of the album’s mix and sonic qualities oscillate between warmth and intimacy and coldness and harshness. Many of the album's sounds have an industrial quality, but they all come through the mix with analog-like warmth and clarity. Primary vocalist Azulay’s spoken-word vocals on tracks like “DIN” sound as if he is an unwell man standing right next to you on the subway, calmly detailing his mental deterioration in broken sentences. At other times, Azulay’s vocals explode into ranting and raving fury, such as during the tortured refrain in the middle and end of “Plasticine.” The opening guitars on “Ergo/Ogre” are subdued jabs, cutting into the mix like a cold butter knife. But that guitar contrasts wildly with the clanky, claustrophobic walls of chaotic distortion that envelop the listener in the song’s more climactic moments. Other aspects of the production are more subtle, such as the kick drum in “Glory Hole” that suddenly has more gain added to it during the song’s climax. According to the band, Slagroom explores “the concept of duality and the conflicts that arise from the battle of opposites,” and that notion is represented in nearly every aspect of the album. Slagroom is a rewarding but unsettling listening experience in part because the result of so many of those “battles of the opposite” is purgatory — a sense of being perpetually stuck in the gray, struggling to answer questions on identity, capitalism, and fame. But this, along with the experimentation and assiduous attention to detail, is what makes Slagroom such an intriguing listen and one of the most engaging noise rock releases this year. Of all the innovative releases put out under the noise rock banner this year, Slagroom is easily one of the best. SLAGROOM by tankerlow

items._cn_summary: 这是乐队第二张专辑，展现出对噪音摇滚边界的拓展。多首曲目以类似嗡鸣的方式缓慢展开，留出足够的呼吸空间，体现出在以密集著称的类型中难得的克制力。制作上经过两年精细打磨，混音在温暖亲密与冰冷严酷之间摆动，呈现出模拟质感的高清晰度。人声处理富于变化，从口语化的低沉独白到爆裂式的狂怒嘶喊，形成强烈张力。编曲融合了锤击扬琴、降调循环人声充当号角、录音中意外产生的反馈等多种非常规元素，每首曲目都保有独立性格。专辑在声音设计层面具有工业质感与实验色彩，对偏好先锋与跨界融合的听众具有较高吸引力。

items.body: The German duo Grimoire De Occulte has been active for several years now and has released the majority of its work, particularly in recent years. Inspired by Bernd Hermanns, aka ‘Baal’ (owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen and also active in several other projects), and ‘Philosoph’, they originally released this album in 2025, with the CD version following this year. The title word ‘Ajna’ undoubtedly refers to the Sanskrit word usually translated as ‘perceiving’, ‘knowing’, or ‘insight’. It also represents the sixth chakra, which is associated with the so-called third eye. This aligns perfectly with the approach of this project, which has always been closely linked to ritual and mysticism. We are presented with an elaborate and unique track lasting nearly 40 minutes. “Ajna: Transmissions” invites the listener to immerse themselves in an esoteric world in which the ‘other side’ plays a prominent role. This naturally provides inspiration for a dark composition, with the duo presenting us with a persistent, ominous wave of sound. At first glance, it may seem somewhat monotonous, yet the composition is enriched with humming sound effects and additional sounds, including all kinds of crackling field recordings. The whole piece is also punctuated by a scream, which adds extra power to the dark ritual. As far as I’m concerned, a few additional tracks could have been included here, but this extended “Ajna: Transmissions” remains a pleasant listen nonetheless. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Anja: Transmissions”: Ajna: Transmissions by Grimoire De Occulte About Grimoire De Occulte Grimoire De Occulte is a German duo formed by Bernd Hermanns, also known as “Baal” and the owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen, together with “Philosoph”. The project’s discography traces back to the 2011 cassette EP “Funeral Lands” on Dunkelheit Produktionen, followed by the self-released 2012 rehearsal tape “Rehearsal November 2012″ and the 2017 split 7” “Dschinn… / Atardecer De Mayo” with Mirthless, also on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Further releases include “Ritual Before Thy Fullmoon (Rehearsal)” (2017) and the self-released cassette “Calling The Ancient Fears” (2021), before the duo returned to Dunkelheit Produktionen for the CD album “Sinister Rituals” (2023) and now “Ajna: Transmissions”, issued digitally in 2025 and on CD in 2026.

items._cn_summary: 德国二人组 Grimoire De Occulte 由厂牌主理人 Baal 与 Philosoph 组成，长期深耕仪式与神秘主义主题。本专辑以梵语「Ajna」（即第三眼脉轮）为概念核心，构建一段近四十分钟的单一长篇作品。整体以持续不断的低频暗潮音墙为骨架，叠加哼鸣音效、噼啪作响的田野录音及突如其来的尖叫采样，营造出阴森压抑的仪式空间感。作品结构上偏向极简主义式的绵延展开，虽略显单调，但声音层次的设计服务于其所追求的通灵与超验体验。该作为独立小厂牌发行，体现了地下暗潮场景对自我仪式美学的坚持，适合需要沉浸式氛围体验的听众。

items.body: Mental wormholes in the night Strange ideas give a familiar fright Some phantom power pulling you back And onto a completely different track Jack Duckworth has spent years making Soft Riot records that seem to know exactly how ridiculous modern life is, then politely invite the machines responsible over for dinner. On his latest LP, Crux, out now through Possession Records and Minimalkombinat, that dinner appears to have taken a turn. Somebody has started transmitting instructions through the walls, and Duckworth is sitting there with a synthesizer trying to determine whether the voice belongs to inspiration, paranoia, technology, or some unseen bastard who has been rewriting his lines while he sleeps. Ghostwriter sets the idea in motion with a Motorik beat, clipped electronics, and Duckworth’s sprechstimme delivered with the disciplinary authority of someone reading factory regulations during an evacuation. There is something of Nitzer Ebb and Suicide in the chant, Fad Gadget in the nervous intelligence, and Skinny Puppy in the sense that electronic equipment might eventually develop opinions about its owner. Elsewhere, the stylish severity of Japan, Bill Nelson’s eccentric futurism, Simple Minds before stadiums swallowed them, and late-period Wire all seem to inhabit the same crooked apartment building. Prince lurks somewhere downstairs, idly wondering why everybody is dressed so seriously. The song concerns creation becoming possession. Ideas appear without explanation, strange mental tunnels open after dark, and ordinary thought gets interrupted by transmissions whose sender remains unknown. Duckworth turns writer’s intuition into supernatural interference: inspiration as somebody else grabbing the steering wheel. His video makes that concept gloriously physical. Forget the standard musician-stares-meaningfully-at-camera routine. Duckworth does that, but becomes part of a universe of printed graphics, hand animation, projected textures, surreal juxtapositions, and visual jokes that recall Dada photomontage, Saul Bass title sequences, and the wonderfully deranged graphic vocabulary of 80s television. Everything looks cut, pasted, shoved sideways, photographed again, and allowed to misbehave. All animations were made physically, with printed graphics manipulated by hand, while projector imagery was filmed again to produce the backgrounds and textures. Duckworth handled the graphics and editing, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. That analogue process becomes part of the argument: “This allowed me not only to get off the computer for most of the creation of this video, but also opened up the doors really wide for collaboration with other people in a far more intuitive and inclusive way,” says Duckworth. “This allowed the usage of computer software to be basic and minimal, mainly keying out backgrounds, levels, colourising and layering of the animated footage. As I feel the world of what I recognize as an underground music scene and community keeps getting more absorbed into the world of statistics, data and marketing that is more in line with late-stage capitalism, it was important for me to focus on things in the real world like working with other people, meeting new ones, connecting with people, traveling and performing live. The digital world today is planned, created, and orchestrated by the corporations that build it — a far cry from the more utopian possibilities the internet held when I first got acquainted with it in the 90s. The physical world, however, is something that we still don’t know the purpose of yet, despite thousands of years of humans trying to speculate why it exists. Ultimately, the digital world we’ve created can’t exist without the physical world it sits in — not the other way around.” Watch the video for Ghostwriter below: With Ghostwriter Jack Duckworth has made a song about invisible influence while creating its visual counterpart with scissors, paper, projectors, hands, and other people. In an era increasingly obsessed with converting creativity into metrics, his forthcoming album Crux finds Soft Riot asking a useful question: when an idea suddenly appears inside your head, who exactly handed it to you? Listen to Ghostwriter below and order Crux here. items._cn_summary: Soft Riot 的新专辑《Crux》探讨创作与占有之间的模糊地带。Jack Duckworth 以 Motorik 节拍、切割式电子音色与德语念白式人声构建歌曲，灵感来源涉及 Nitzer Ebb、Suicide、Fad Gadget、Skinny Puppy 等后朋克与工业先驱，同时融入 Japan 的冷峻优雅、Bill Nelson 的怪异未来主义以及 Wire 的解构意识。歌词将灵感转化为超自然干扰——想法在深夜涌现，如同某位隐形者篡改了意识轨迹。配套 MV 采用全实物手工动画：印刷图形被手作操纵，投影影像再经摄影转译为背景与纹理，辅以达达主义拼贴、Saul Bass 式片头美学与八十年代电视的视觉语汇。Duckworth 强调脱离电脑主导的创作方式，以实现更直觉化的人际协作。整体呈现出对机器时代潜意识入侵的戏谑而不安的回应。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
