items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑由鼓手 Gerry Hemingway 领衔，集合德国多管乐手 Frank Gratkowski、爱尔兰钢琴家 Izumi Kimura 与瑞士贝斯手 Christian Weber 四位国际乐手，在瑞士 Altbüron 的 Bau 4 木材厂空间录制。曲目以长篇即兴为主，穿插预谱段落，木料废料被用作打击与敲击声源，构成独特的音色层。Hemingway 的作曲延续了他在 Anthony Braxton 四重奏时期的经验，擅长以非对称乐句、叙事性段落编排与子组合对话搭建结构。钢琴–鼓二重奏《Third Story Variation》以呼吸般的脉动与准备内化钢琴技法紧密交织，三重奏《Slivers》则在低音单簧管与弓弦贝斯的对位中展开。评论既肯定了编排的即时机智与音色默契，也指出鼓手在长篇展开中偶尔力度不足、摇摆感松弛的问题。

items.body: Anyone who’s spent time in large train stations late at night or early in the morning, before the commuter rush and the busy timetables begin, will have noticed that they are quite unique sonic environments. Vast and cavernous, open at both ends, with a proliferation of hard surfaces, and heavy machinery coming and going, central stations play host to a range of interesting acoustic phenomena: resonating eddies of wind, reverberant chugging of diesel and electric engines, and echoing clatters and clamours of all sorts. Amsterdam’s central station is a prime example of such an environment, and Cinema Perdu’s latest album is both named after and created in response to it. I’m not sure how many of the sounds on the album were derived from recordings made in the station, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it was 100%. For all I know, even the melancholic string-like chords and pitched tones used here and there could have been created through some sort of filtering of recorded sound; at any rate, they sound natural, part of the whole, rather than like add-ons. The liner notes state that the intention was not to accurately document or recreate the sounds of the station as they are heard directly, and apart from a few vague snatches of tannoy announcements, obvious sonic signifiers are avoided. Yet the impression created is very much one of a large train station: the hissing and ringing, the rumble and clatter, the quiet screeches, the billowing wind, and the general hubbub all seem instantly familiar. Often this seems to have as much to do with how the sounds change as much as their qualities at any one moment. The way the quiet ambient gleams and glimmers of the opening track breathe slowly in an out, as if we were listening to the respiration of the station, is but one example of this. Or perhaps that sense of familiarity stems from the music’s ability to evoke not only the sounds of a large central train station, but also the unique state of consciousness provoked by being in one. Regular visitors to such stations will know what I mean. There’s that sense of self-effacement, of merging with the environment; the intimate yet fleeting connections with hundreds of strangers; the endless waiting. On the album’s final track, rumble, ring, and clatter slowly build, before being overtaken by soft distortion. Hiss, clamour, and the billowing of wind create a slow-moving chaos. A glimmering chord slowly blossoms and sweeps the chaos away, like the rolling to a halt of the train that will take you home. Central train stations leave unique and indelible marks on the psyche, and “Amsterdam CS” traces those marks with skill and careful attentiveness. [bandcamp width=100% height=120 album=909022375 size=large bgcol=ffffff linkcol=0687f5 tracklist=false artwork=small track=3742585179] Cinema Perdu Moving Furniture Records

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以阿姆斯特丹中央火车站为创作灵感与声源素材，深度探索大型交通枢纽独特的声学空间特质。创作者通过现场录音捕捉车站中风的对流回旋、引擎的混响轰鸣、各种金属撞击与回声，将这些原始声响转化为音乐素材，而非简单还原环境音。专辑刻意回避直接的广播通知等显性标志，却通过声音的渐变、呼吸般的节奏与缓慢的层次堆叠，营造出车站特有的声场氛围与心理状态——那种自我消融于环境的感受、与无数陌生人擦肩而过的瞬时连接、以及无尽等待的意识体验。最终曲目中轰鸣、铃声与喧嚣逐渐被柔光般的和弦取代，象征列车缓缓到站、归途开启的尾声。整张作品以精确的听觉敏感度与艺术构思，刻画了中央车站在人类心理上留下的独特印记。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生、驻肯尼亚的打击乐手 Sven Kacirek 与搭档 Olith Ratengo 共同创作，并邀请83岁肯尼亚东部传统歌手 Ogoya Nengo 加盟，构成跨代际、跨文化的三角组合。Kacirek 以 Buchla 合成器、手打打击乐与偶尔的架子鼓构建节奏底层，与人声形成精妙的悬浮关系——合成器层叠的复合节奏从最初显得生硬的对位，逐渐与歌声融为一体，仿佛一直潜藏在声部之下。曲目如《Sarah》中，电子元素以扭曲质地在人声高潮处悄然渗入，强化紧迫感而不喧宾夺主。专辑标题中的「dodo」传统与电子制作并行，体现传统根源在当代语境中被重新激活的过程。这类创作展示了不同文化之间真诚对话的可能：根脉成为前卫，创新看似古老千年。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._genre: world fusion / homemade instruments / experimental folk / klezmer / cumbia
items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑以手工自制的乐器为核心特色。他们将日常废弃物改造为功能完备的乐器——包括低音管、笛类、非洲鼓模仿品甚至厨房用具，每件都经过精确调音，在现代录音技术下呈现出丰富的音质。作品风格跨越多种世界音乐传统：开篇以犹太克莱兹默风格引入单簧管旋律与低音管伴奏；哥伦比亚昆比亚曲目中西班牙合唱与拉丁打击乐交织；非洲节奏段落采用木鱼、沙锤与摇铃构建层次；桑巴旋律展现长笛技巧；中东调式则营造出六十年代间谍片配乐般的恍惚氛围。所有作品均由自创乐器演奏，编曲在即兴段落中展现出扎实的演奏功底，是一张融合世界音乐元素与手工声音实验的跨界作品。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter Live at Still Point 2026 by Ian Hawgood   A live album promises to bear witness, a weighty claim, perhaps too weighty. It evokes the idea of an event fixed once and for all, destined to return unchanged with every listen. Live At Still Point 2026 favors a memory with sections erased, passages heard only by those present at Brimscombe Mill that afternoon. The recording preserves the core of Ian Hawgood’s performance, while the contributions of two laptops used for processing were never captured in the file. A tangible absence, then, which has become the defining character of the work itself. The released sound recognizes its own limits and reveals them with rare candor. For Hawgood, the concert marked his return to performing before an audience after seven years. That fact carries more weight than a line in a press release, since his artistic journey has always sought a human dimension in the act of listening. A British sound engineer, founder of Home Normal and custodian of Folk Reels, he has built an extensive catalog around care, collaboration, tape and field recordings. At Still Point, that principle reconnects with the risk of the moment and a freedom still capable of play. Twenty five minutes, a single movement. At first come rustling sounds, calls whose source is difficult to place, brief electrical flashes. They​ resemble tentative contacts taking the measure of the air. Then a deep mass expands, gathering everything happening around it. Figures from We Are But Dream are bent and pushed towards a different sense of duration. Hawgood uses SYNTRX, Buchla sequences, sounds gathered outdoors and computers running AudioMulch, instruments from different eras surrendering their names to a single current. The music grows unhurriedly and gathers body through accumulation. A melody seems about to declare itself, then immediately chooses a less determinate form. This hesitation gives the work its intensity. No backdrop inviting distraction, no contemplative postcard. Hawgood’s ambient music asks for attention in a low voice and makes perceptible the time sound requires to change its nature. From time to time, an impulse punctures the continuity, an oblique jolt roughens the balance. It happens, that is all. The performance retains a vulnerable quality, even a slight awkwardness, precious in an age obsessed with polish. Depth becomes almost physical :: In the central stretch, depth becomes almost physical. The volume rises, the fabric thickens, while the pressure avoids all monumental emphasis. Hawgood proceeds through successive degrees of proximity: one colour enters another, the drone slowly alters its light, the breathing becomes irregular. It takes time to realize that the initial landscape is already elsewhere. At the point of greatest rarefaction, the current loses substance and seems about to fade out. The music accepts this descent. From there emerge more clearly defined figures, a gentle pulse, circling scales that bring energy without breaking the spell. The ending gathers motion and a strange, purposeful serenity, as though the sound had found a way to continue after almost dispersing. Tim Diagram’s photograph translates this condition well. Trees seen from below, pale clouds, a second pattern of foliage superimposed upon the sky. The image holds two temporalities and allows them to interfere. The album likewise contains what happens and the imprint of what escapes. The material lost from the two computers compels a reconsideration of what a document can mean. The audience heard a broader version, traversed by elements that are now irretrievable; the album offers an autonomous trajectory, barer and perhaps more exposed. Fidelity lies in the gesture, its openness to chance and the human scale of what has been preserved. Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. The still point evoked by the title becomes a magnetic centre around which everything changes: intensity, distance, density, memory. This is where the album’s achievement lies. Its beauty arises from a restrained decision: to release what survived without consoling reconstruction and to entrust absence with an active role. At the end, an unusual feeling lingers. Has one listened to a concert, or to the memory that a concert produced inside a machine? The question matters more than any answer. Hawgood offers twenty five minutes freed from the pose of the celebratory live album and the smoothness of the ambient product. The sound breathes, falters, gathers strength and recedes. In that movement it carries with it the Still Point community, the apprehension of returning, the pleasure of experimentation and the part that no medium will ever be able to hold. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter. Live at Still Point 2026 is available on folk reels. items.body: Review by alainPP — Green Carnation presents the third album in the "A Dark Poem" trilogy, nodding to the likes of Anathema and Katatonia. It delivers an oppressive, heavy, and meditative sound with dark progressive roots."Unconditional Artificial Chemistry" opens with a spacey feel, suddenly cut through by an exuberant, thick, heavy guitar; the monolithic vocals help transport the listener to another planet. The track narrates the dangers of AI, unfolding seamlessly while building an all-encompassing, progressive intensity. It shifts to include a crystalline piano in the distance, with musical grandeur that straddles the line between doom and Opeth-esque gothic metal, creating an oppressive atmosphere. There is a spellbinding melancholy'a blend of Anathema, Mogwai, Katatonia, and early King Crimson. "The Messiah Complex" features a melting guitar arpeggio, with vocals that abruptly break the ethereal, charming, and hypnotic mood. Melancholic, mysterious keyboards add a layer of solemnity that oozes progressive structure, while the dominant vocals allow the mantra-like atmosphere to spill over. The decrescendo finale is simple and effective'steady and unstoppable'serving as a musical paradigm."Broken Souls, Common Enemies" features a prominent New Wave-style synth driving the rhythm. The riff, the languid vocals, and the guitar's plaintive melody evoke emotion, discovery, and complexity in a track that is heavy without flaunting it. A shift to screamed vocals over a machine-gun riff'reminiscent of The Gathering in their early days'reasserts the track's intensity and complexity, bolstered by Wright-esque keyboards. A break featuring an ethereal flute and a melting, Western-style acoustic solo follows. Vocoded vocals amplify the majestic atmosphere, launching a stratospheric guitar solo worthy of the genre's titans'a truly stunning moment. Finally, "A Dark Poem - Orchestral Suite" begins with otherworldly vocals introducing wind instruments'including Ingrid's flute'as the orchestral arrangement takes center stage. An orchestral suite worthy of *Fantasia*'a classic pastoral anthem recounting Rimbaud's "Ophelia," performed by the Kristiansand Symphony Orchestra and its opera choir. Then comes the break: a return to archaic vocals, a primal sound reaching its zenith'is this the birth of prog? A dark, unsettling, yet colorful and pastoral atmosphere, pierced by illuminating trumpets; it is a masterpiece right up to the final note, with a soaring violin flourish creating a moment that transcends time.Green Carnation takes its final bow with this triptych finale'punchier, spellbinding, and invigorating. It is a crowning achievement, blending dystopian lyrics about our society with majestic, solemn melodies. Classy, ​​dreamlike, and immense progressive post-metal'featuring a sound that left an indelible mark on me from their very beginnings, delivering a powerful impact this September.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Green Carnation「黑暗诗篇」三部曲的终章，整体呈现出沉重、冥想且带有黑暗前卫根基的氛围。专辑融合了Anathema式的忧郁、Katatonia的灰暗、Opeth的哥特金属气质以及Mogwai的后摇张力，编曲在厄运金属与前卫金属之间游走。曲目中大量运用管弦乐编排，由Kristiansand交响乐团及歌剧合唱团演绎，引入笛子、小提琴、号等古典器乐，与电吉他音墙、新浪潮合成器、嘶吼人声并置。键盘层次营造出催眠般的氛围，吉他独奏被描述为具有该流派巨人级别的水准。终曲「黑暗诗篇-管弦乐组曲」以兰波的「奥菲利亚」为文本，构建出牧歌式的庄严景观。歌词触及AI危险、社会反乌托邦等主题，整体兼具沉重感与恢弘的旋律性。

items.body: I’ll always wait for you The promise that someone will wait forever has enjoyed an excellent reputation in love songs, considering how uncomfortable it can become outside them. Patience can deepen into devotion, but it can also give obsession an alibi, allowing someone to call an inability to let go proof of a superior kind of love. London trio Black Doldrums explore that uneasy territory on Waiting, a song whose tenderness comes with the unnerving suggestion that nobody has agreed on when the waiting should come to an end. The third single from Repetition Compulsion, due November 13th, 2026, via Fuzz Club, carries a particular connection to the band’s previous album. Written around the same time as In Limerence, it extends that record’s preoccupation with longing and romantic fixation into a love song that sounds both consoling and quietly bereft. Its accompanying video takes those feelings out into the city, where a solitary attachment becomes an increasingly threatening pursuit. A deep, humming bass and the heavy thud of drums establish the song’s measured pace, while a cool, jangling guitar melody moves between high, glassy notes and lower, mournful phrases. There is something of The Chameleons in the guitar’s arcing melodies, and of The Cure in the funereal weight beneath it. Sheets of icy synthesizer widen the space around the instruments, giving the opening a peculiar calm: everything sounds composed, even as the melody suggests that something has gone terribly wrong. When Kevin Gibbard begins singing, the synthesizers settle into warmer mid-range tones, bringing a little bodily comfort to that cold room. His voice carries some of Andrew Eldritch’s solemn authority in a slightly higher register, with an exposed ache that also recalls Ian Curtis. Beneath him, the guitar takes on an increasingly Cure-like character, its clear notes ringing against the low end. Then the chorus rises into “I’ll always wait for you,” stretching the promise into a lament. The guitar’s answering jangle supplies the small, involuntary chill, the sort that travels up an arm before the mind has decided whether the feeling is pleasure or dread. For all that unease, the song began in an ordinary moment of affection. Gibbard wrote the lyrics early one morning while waiting for Sophie Landers to wake up, with the themes of their second album still close at hand. “When we were going through the finished mixes of the second album, Sophie noticed this recurring theme of limerence, which pushed ‘Waiting’ further in that direction. I liked the idea of writing about waiting for someone you love, that if you love someone enough, you’ll wait forever. I wrote all the lyrics in one go, early one morning, while I was literally waiting for Sophie to wake up. I just started jotting it down.” Landers also supplied the idea behind one of the recording’s stranger details, asking for a sound that would suggest a spirit departing its body. Gibbard found his approximation through a Mellotron, voice synthesizers, and pitch bend: “Sophie wanted something that sounded like a soul leaving someone’s body. So I played around with a Mellotron and voice synths with pitch bend to create something similar. It seemed to fit nicely because it has this really haunting sound.” That imagined departure hangs over a song devoted to staying. The warmer synthesizers offer closeness, while the guitars and spectral vocal textures suggest distance, absence, and the possibility that a promise might outlast the person it was made to. There is considerable romance in Waiting, though very little reassurance that romance will make anyone happy. The video’s darker premise took shape during a recent viewing of Taxi Driver. Landers recognized connections between the film and the band’s interest in limerence, particularly its treatment of loneliness, idealization, mental distress, and destructive fixation. Black Doldrums developed those observations into a story about an isolated, obsessive man following a woman through the city, with his sense of control destined for a nasty correction. Gibbard and Landers occupy a nocturnal world of café booths, shuttered shopfronts, graffiti-covered brickwork, and stretches of nearly empty pavement. He sits alone with a cup, writes on a loose sheet of paper, and eats in a café; she walks through the streets in a black leather jacket, occasionally looking back. The editing brings their separate movements into an uncomfortable relationship, while red-lit close-ups of her eyes interrupt the greenish darkness outside. The ordinary business of getting through a night begins to feel charged with the possibility of being watched. As the distance between them closes, the action moves into a narrow pedestrian underpass, its fluorescent lights leaving little room for either figure to disappear. Landers walks ahead while Gibbard follows, until a look back changes the balance between pursuer and pursued. The closing image gives heartbreak an abruptly physical form, making the familiar business of giving someone your heart seem like an offer best considered carefully. Watch the video for Waiting below: Gibbard and Landers formed Black Doldrums in London, initially working as a duo built around guitar, drums, and vocals before expanding into a trio. Their 2022 debut Dead Awake and 2024 follow-up In Limerence, both released through Fuzz Club, brought their early interests in psychedelia, drone, and reverb into a more concentrated gothic post-punk form. Extensive UK and European touring followed, including arena dates supporting Archive and their own headline shows. Repetition Compulsion completes the band’s interconnected “State of Mind Trilogy,” exploring the emotional patterns people carry into relationships, memory, and self-understanding. Across eleven songs, the record expands those concerns into inherited behaviour, politics, and mental wellbeing. Waiting provides a particularly intimate connection between the trilogy’s final two chapters, holding affection and fixation close enough for their resemblance to become unsettling. The album arrives November 13th, 2026, on 180-gram neon-yellow vinyl limited to 350 hand-numbered copies, 180-gram ultra-clear vinyl, and CD. Pre-order the album here. Listen below and order via Bandcamp. items.album: Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR Explore Faith, Fear, and the Frailty of Flesh on Gothic Post-Punk LP “Eaten of Worms”

items.body: His curved neck bent right back to see the swan Dreading the four steps up and over to where we ran I reached the viewing point and I sit here watching and waiting But then sometimes life’s unkind Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR makes post-punk as though somebody locked Ladytron in an abandoned theater with a deathrock band, a stack of Killing Joke records, several reels of damaged fairy-tale film, and instructions that nobody gets out until dawn. Somewhere behind the electronic throb and serrated guitar on their latest offering, the EATEN OF WORMS LP, there is also the emotional breadth of the Chameleons, a little Breeders crookedness, and that marvelous early-goth conviction on bass guitar. The band began with best friends playing and dancing in a dark Boston basement at the tail end of the pandemic, drawing together members of The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz, and Secret Hearts. They describe this incarnation as their “dark punk chapter,” which sounds about right, though “chapter” seems almost too civilized for music filled with drowning sailors, torn bodies, predatory birds, collapsing circuses, religious dread, and people standing beside freezing seas wondering precisely when existence developed such a personal vendetta. There are obvious ancestral spirits here: Xmal Deutschland, Parálisis Permanente, early Siouxsie and the Banshees, the strange congregation that gathered around the London Batcave when punk discovered it could wear theatrical makeup without surrendering its teeth. They sound less interested in reconstructing 1982 than in asking what happens when those old poisons get poured into present-day arteries. Their live pedigree adds another clue. GOSSIP COLLAR have shared stages with The March Violets, Pink Turns Blue, Rendez-Vous, Haunt Me, House of Harm, Fotocrime, and Sympathy Flowers, placing them comfortably among bands for whom darkness still needs rhythm, muscle, and enough propulsion to keep bodies moving even while the songs are busy describing spiritual ruin. Throughout the songs on EATEN OF WORMS, nature rarely provides comfort. Seas threaten to swallow people, birds wait for flesh, wolves pursue deer, plants cut skin, rain destroys, and the night contains forces that clearly have not received the memo about personal boundaries. GOSSIP COLLAR’s apocalyptic fairy tale grows out of this collision between childhood imagery and adult terror, where forests, animals, oceans, and old religious symbols have all turned slightly hostile. Edgar Froese once said, “There is no death, there is just a change of our cosmic address.” GOSSIP COLLAR sound perfectly capable of furnishing the house he moved into. Disguise My Heart opens with a saxophone-like drone, its low complaint quickly overtaken by a deep, quick-moving bassline and drums that strike with the urgent physical force of Joy Division’s Love Will Tear Us Apart. The guitars pick out a cold, melodic figure before heavier layers gather around it, giving the song a density that makes the vocal seem to travel from somewhere beyond the instruments. Witchy and windblown, the voice calls through the mix with a banshee’s sense of occasion, stretching the distance between the rhythm section’s forward charge and the solitary figure waiting beside the Northern Sea. Freezing water, aching eyes, and blood threatening to turn cold give emotional injury a bodily presence; the guitars seem to press against the skin as insistently as the memories. Even as the drums push onward, the song remains fixed on that desolate stretch of coastline. Heartbreak becomes architectural here: eventually you stop carrying it around and simply move into it. Scavengers follows with a sheet of cold guitar and an insistent bass throb, burying an unusually inviting melody several layers into the disturbance. When the arrangement briefly catches its breath, the bass leads the voice into view, exposing the sharp, declamatory cadence beneath its witchy inflections. There is an anarcho-punk edge to the delivery, a sense that these words are being hurled across a room even as the guitars make that room feel enormous. That force suits a song whose speaker lies broken, bleeding, and apparently available to whatever happens to be circling overhead. The hook keeps drawing the ear back through the commotion while memories collect like personal debris beside the body. Death may happen quickly, destruction takes its time, and the promise of resurrection supplies a final complication. Apparently even carrion birds are going to have to wait their turn. A brief arc of distortion introduces Big Top Comes Crashing Down, followed by a jagged guitar figure that rings with the blunt insistence of a tolling bell. Once the drums and bass hit, the riff acquires a crooked melodic momentum, turning its initial severity into something almost indecently catchy. Above it, the vocal echoes with a thunderous breadth, making the performance feel much larger than the cramped emotional circumstances it describes. White greasepaint goes on, the smile gets rehearsed again, and another day disappears beneath the effort of remaining presentable. That circling guitar figure becomes an apt accompaniment to the work of doing it all again tomorrow. The image of someone maintaining the same expression for ten years on Exmouth Street carries the ugly comedy of a photograph that has outlived everybody’s patience. Keep smiling hard enough and sooner or later your face becomes part of the prison. Haerisis gives the bass room to announce itself, opening with a thick, deliberate strut locked to the drumbeat. Sustained guitar tones spread above that steady march, and the clearer placement of the vocal lets its chanting insistence register more directly. The arrangement has a substantial physical weight, with dense guitar chords and more melodic lines carrying on around a groove that remains easy to follow through all the theological panic. Blood, broken bones, forbidden chalices, frozen streams, wolves, and deer crowd the lyrics, turning belief into a landscape where almost everything can injure you. The sustained tones lend those images a sense of scale, while the rhythm section keeps their violence close enough to feel. There is something particularly effective about the orderly tread beneath all this religious dread: the song advances with the certainty of a procession whose destination nobody has thought to question. On Dead Thing, a heavy wash of guitar gives way to the splash and momentum of the drums, with the opening density settling into a firm support for the melody. Another weighty riff sweeps through the arrangement, while a persistent guitar drone keeps pressure on the spaces between its movements. The vocal sounds cavernous, its thunderous resonance making each phrase seem to return from the far end of a large, inhospitable room. Those overlapping guitar textures give the song’s fascination with self-destruction considerable force. Lions are led by their manes, weapons are made, and human ingenuity eventually discovers the convenience of turning its own inventions inward. Scars become evidence and shame becomes inheritance, yet the drums maintain enough movement to make the plea for dancing feel entirely plausible. Tenderness enters through the side door wearing funeral clothes, and the rhythm section has already made room for it. Why Me? begins with eerie chimes and a low drone, suggesting an old piano being played somewhere beyond the inhabited rooms of a house. A thick bass figure gradually establishes the song’s tension, recalling the stalking movement of the Cure’s A Forest with considerably more weight behind each step. The vocal holds its heat close, sounding troubled and intimate against the spacious opening. Around the halfway point, heavier guitars enter and the arrangement settles into a cold gothic-rock groove, increasing the pressure while keeping its movements controlled. That restraint gives the lyrics’ grotesque physical imagery additional bite. Red lips, internal screaming, and organs hanging from trees turn desire into a form of captivity, while the bass continues its patient inspection. The fascination directed toward the speaker feels increasingly forensic, as though somebody has been pinned beneath a collector’s glass and asked to appreciate the compliment. The uneasy string-like tones and warbles that open Peaceful in Daylight make its title seem optimistic well before the kick drum lands. Arcs of cold guitar stretch across the entrance, then the full beat pushes the song into motion, carrying heavy riffs and a vocal whose witchy bite grows sharper against the instrumental weight. Seaweed, dense smoke, cutting thorns, broken walls, injured skin, and abandoned nests accumulate in the lyrics, filling the song with evidence that something has gone badly wrong. The arrangement gives that damaged environment a restless physical life; every forward push seems to uncover another unpleasant detail. An old-school rock guitar solo adds a flash of theatrical excess, briefly letting the instrument take over the voice’s fevered work. Daylight may make this place easier to inspect, but there is very little in the music to suggest that inspection will bring reassurance. Spelling Misery initially gives its guitar melody a clear view of the room. The figure rises and falls over a solid rhythm section, its easy memorability providing a point of reference before heavier guitars and dark vocals crowd into the arrangement. Further melodic details appear as the song progresses, with a recurring gothic-rock guitar phrase adding small complications to the surrounding force. Those returns keep the ear attached to the song even as its family portrait becomes increasingly difficult to look at. Anger lives in the blood, a father kills the fatted calf in nervous rage, and memory falters under the effort of naming what has happened. Biblical promises of shelter follow: arrows will fail, feathers will cover the vulnerable body, and fear might be held outside for another night. The returning guitar figure offers a little steadiness amid those appeals, though the heavier passages make the promised protection feel precarious. Unsafe State opens with a buzzing synthesizer pulse and cold electronic tones, briefly suggesting a turn toward synthwave before the melodic resonance of the post-punk guitars establishes its place on the record. The vocal sits more clearly in the mix, and its somber delivery makes the song’s vulnerability unusually exposed. Where other tracks enlarge their distress through dense guitars and cavernous echoes, this one allows the words to feel nearer, with the electronic repetition giving them an uneasy regularity. Eyes lose their rhythm, time becomes a dark tunnel, and the speaker digs until their nails hurt while dead souls call from somewhere nearby. The guitar melody carries that distress with a fragile clarity, giving the song an emotional directness that makes its domestic setting especially troubling. Home is supposed to provide some distance from danger; here, danger has apparently obtained a key. The closing Merchants of the Wave begins with a bassline that shifts up and down, setting a rolling motion beneath a classic post-punk guitar figure. Broader gothic-rock arcs develop around that melody, while the ghostly vocal seems suspended above the rhythm section’s steady movement. The arrangement gives the record’s returning ocean imagery a physical shape: friends venture onto dangerous seas, boats pitch, beds shake with frantic dreams, and tears become indistinguishable from salt water. The bass keeps the song moving beneath those anxious visions, its rises and falls suggesting the uncertain footing of people trying to remain upright. Prayer repeats because repetition may be the only available defense against forces too large to negotiate with. The sea that opened the album as a place of private emotional exposure becomes a shared source of fear here, carrying the possibility that somebody loved might disappear beyond reach. GOSSIP COLLAR keeps returning to bodies under pressure: freezing, bleeding, scratched, exposed, dissected, exhausted, threatened with consumption or drowning. Yet these bodies persist. They dance. They pray. They disguise themselves. They paint their faces. They get abandoned to scavengers and announce plans to rise anyway. Musically, that stubbornness comes through in the combination of deathrock abrasion and electronic precision. Imagine Ladytron discovering a box of Killing Joke singles beneath the floorboards, then recruiting the Chameleons to widen the horizon while somebody from the Breeders quietly rearranges the furniture. Beneath all the gothic architecture runs punk’s ancient belief that anxiety becomes considerably more useful once somebody gives it a bassline. That may be why GOSSIP COLLAR’s particular apocalypse remains so inviting. Civilization has collapsed, the circus tent is falling, the sea wants your body, God may or may not be answering correspondence, and several animals appear to have questionable intentions. Fine. There is still a song playing downstairs. Might as well dance before the scavengers get here. Listen to EATEN OF WORMS below and order the album, out now via Bat-Cave Productions, here. items.body: Label: Edition Records, 2026 Personnel - Mark Guiliana: drums, percussion, electronics, keyboards, guitar, vocals; Nicholas Semrad: keyboards; Stu Brooks: electric bass (#3), electronics (#2,4,7,8); Tim Lefebvre: electric bass (#2,4,6); Gretchen Parlato: vocals (#4,5); Marley Guiliana: vocals (#5). Mixed feelings arose from listening to Beat Music 2.0 , the synth-infused follow-up to Mark Guiliana’s Grammy-nominated album Beat Music! Beat Music! Beat Music! (Motéma, 2019). Retro and futuristic waves emerge from Guiliana’s compositions, which draw inspiration from early gaming culture and electronic music. Still, the focus here is on human connection and collaboration, as he enlists keyboardist Nicholas Semrad, bassist Tim Lefebvre, vocalist Gretchen Parlato, and Stu Brooks on electronics. The opener, “ B.ANG ”, excavates retro electronic music through glitchy synth ostinatos that march alongside the harmonic progression, along with a mix of ambient undercurrents and Gary Numan-style electro-rock energy. Although it tests the elasticity of the song’s edges, this piece failed to leave a strong impression on me. “ B.ORN ” and “ W.EST ” are also nothing special, while “ D.RUM ”, with its industrial stomp generating controlled trepidation and Parlato’s vocals highlighting the contrasting ambient-leaning passages, has a little more flair. I did feel a spark on numbers like “ P.LAY ”, whose actively propulsive drumming, together with Lefebvre’s brawny bass fluxes and pedals, is nothing short of gravity-defying, and “ B.EAT ”, whose grooving dub atmosphere morphs into club-dance territory for a while. Brooks, who infuses relevant, to-the-point electronics into the former, switches to electric bass on the latter. Also worth mentioning is “ M.OVE ”, whose danceable techno patterns reminded me of 808 State. Cross-rhythmic tides and dramatic shifts make this one a standout. Guiliana’s passion for what he does is undeniable, yet the prevailing virtues of Beat Music 2.0 come to the fore when the layers adopt a less explicit old-school electronic vibe in favor of more modernistic experimentation. Favorite Tracks: 02 - P.LAY ► 03 - B.EAT ► 07 - M.OVE

items._cn_summary: Mark Guiliana继2019年格莱美提名专辑之后的续作，以鼓为核心展开电子与爵士的交叉实验。专辑邀请键盘手Nicholas Semrad、贝斯手Tim Lefebvre、人声Gretchen Parlato及电子乐人Stu Brooks参与，编制灵活多变。多首曲目以简短缩写命名，结构短小，融入复古游戏音乐、808 State式techno模式、dub氛围以及Gary Numan式electro-rock能量，在工业节奏与ambient段落之间来回切换。评论者认为过于直白的复古电子质感削弱了冲击力，而当层次转向更具现代感的实验手法时表现最佳，推荐曲目集中在P.LAY、B.EAT与M.OVE。整体展现了鼓手在电子化语境下对节奏与空间感的探索，是一张介于传统爵士鼓语汇与俱乐部电子舞曲之间的跨界作品。

items.body: A centuries-old devotional song from Morocco’s Gnawa repertoire, “M’Bara Meskin” tells of poor M’Bara, left outside the shrine in torn clothes to brew his tea from leaves others have thrown away. Inside, the Sidi and the Lalla, Moroccan honorifics for a gentleman and a lady, sip theirs in their slippers. Sydney-born multi-instrumentalist Julian Belbachir has rebuilt it on reggae and dub, keeping the vocal in Moroccan Arabic, from sessions in Morocco, Mali, Australia, Canada and Jamaica. Belbachir was born to a Moroccan father and an Australian mother and grew up in Surry Hills and Redfern, where he started on West African drums at five under griots and master drummers from Sydney’s African diaspora. He went on to study percussion and instrument-making in Guinea, Senegal, Mali and Morocco, and plays the kamele n’goni, the harp-lute of Mali’s Wassoulou region. From 2013 to 2022 he drummed for the Australian Indigenous dub band OKA, and after the death of its founder, Stuart “Boga” Fergie, he went solo with his 2022 debut album, Babdoukkala. Gnawa music was carried into Morocco by West Africans brought north across the Sahara, many of them enslaved, and the personnel on his forthcoming album, The Golden Light, follow the same route: more than 30 musicians from Mali and Morocco, among them Moussa Diakite, lead guitarist for Salif Keita. “M’Bara Meskin” came out on 11 September as its first single, with the album due in February 2027. Belbachir hears the song as a portrait of “the hardships musicians face in their daily lives“. The video, shot on Super 8 over two trips to Essaouira three years apart, follows his collaborators through rehearsals, recording sessions and time with their community in the Atlantic port best known for its annual Gnawa festival. items._cn_summary: Julian Belbachir 的单曲取自摩洛哥 Gnawa 传统曲目，以雷鬼与 dub 节奏重构这首数百年历史的宗教歌曲，保留了原版摩洛哥阿拉伯语人声部分。来自悉尼的 Belbachir 拥有摩洛哥与澳大利亚双重文化背景，五岁起在西非鼓乐大师门下学习打击乐，后在几内亚、塞内利、马里和盧洛哥深造，还能演奏马里 Wassoulou 地区的竖琴鲁特琴 kamele n'goni。他曾为澳大利亚原住民 dub 乐队 OKA 担任鼓手九年，乐队创始人去世后于 2022 年发行首张个人专辑。其即将出版的专辑《The Golden Light》汇集了来自马里和盧洛哥的三十多位音乐人，其中包括 Salif Keita 的首席吉他手 Moussa Diakite。Belbachir 将这首歌视为对音乐人在日常生活中所面临艰辛的写照。

items.body: Where’s the joy in this all? Where’s the light in the dark My hands hide my tears, I feel so lost This first day of Fall There is something especially lonely about being miserable on a day for which everyone else has already chosen your mood. A birthday comes with instructions: answer the messages, accept the affection, make a wish. For Los Angeles post-punk duo DECEITS, The First Day of Fall opens up the awful distance between that public celebration and a private wish to disappear. The calendar, as ever, has failed to consult the person concerned. Following our premiere of the single, the song returns with a video directed by Shutter Visual, whose credits include work with Twin Tribes and Blood Club. Its tightly framed performance brings the song’s distress into uncomfortable proximity, with vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Kevin Moreno and drummer Francisco Saenz caught inside a room that seems to grow smaller as the performance intensifies. Moreno wrote the song on a despondent morning the day before his birthday. Faced with an occasion supposedly reserved for happiness, he found himself confronting the desire not to exist at all. That unhappy collision gives the lyrics their particular ache: another year becomes something to account for, while the prospect of celebration makes an already difficult feeling harder to explain. Autumn provides an apt setting for such thoughts, its gradual retreat from summer matching the impulse to withdraw from everyone wishing you well. The arrangement gives those thoughts a restless physical form. A commanding bassline and forceful drums drive through the song, while reverberant guitars spread outward over gothic synthesizers. There is punk urgency in the rhythm section and a wounded romanticism in the melody, each pulling at the other. Moreno’s singing follows the same uneasy course, moving from a softer, intimate register into high, strained cries as the music gathers force. The spacious production leaves room around his voice without taking any pressure off it. Shutter Visual builds the clip around that pressure. Blue-green light washes across the musicians, with hanging guitars, amplifiers, and the white grid beneath their feet giving the performance space a stark, enclosed character. Close-ups of picking hands and struck cymbals keep returning us to the effort involved in playing, while wider shots catch Moreno bending over his guitar and throwing his head back. Saenz’s drumming supplies a firm center as the camera moves between the two. Elsewhere, Moreno faces the lens with dark makeup trailing beneath his eyes, his pale shirt and decorative collar giving way to black stage clothes in other shots. He grips the microphone, raises his hands to his face, and sings with an increasingly exposed intensity. Blurred movement, doubled faces, and fractured views interrupt the more straightforward performance footage, making his expressions difficult to hold in focus. The visual instability suits a song about feeling estranged from the very life everyone else is congratulating you on having. Near the end, the camera settles on white roses and scattered petals across the gridded floor. Against the room’s severe geometry, the flowers look painfully vulnerable, their associations with affection and celebration left in disarray. It is a fitting image for the song’s birthday premise, and Shutter Visual lets the performance carry the desperation that drove Moreno to write it. The most affecting moments come when his gestures seem to outrun his composure, giving visible shape to what the lyrics struggle to contain. Watch the video for The First Day of Fall below: Since forming in Los Angeles in 2021, Moreno and Saenz have channeled their shared love of the Spanish-language music of their upbringing into a particularly expressive strain of post-punk. Its rhythms, romantic feeling, and emotional directness inform a sound that gives gothic reserve very little room to get comfortable. The First Day of Fall draws on that openness, bringing a difficult private experience into a form that other people can recognize and share. The First Day of Fall is out now, with the demo version also included on the Bandcamp release. Listen below and order the single here. The First Day Of Fall by DECEITS DECEITS continue their Hurt As Much As Me Tour through the United States, followed by an appearance at BLOODFLOWERS — Japan Goth & Post Punk Festival in Tokyo and dates in New Zealand and Australia. items.body: Fawning, we’re brighter, we’re cautious, Falling like fighters, we’re caustic. Cracked up like actors, we’re lying. Daydreams and nightmares. Sharing cigarettes and leather trousers can feel like a promising start to eternity, until eternity begins to resemble an argument neither person can leave. Berlin’s Night Nail take that unhappy prospect to the dance floor on Vile Train, a gothic rock seduction in which two lovers become so absorbed in each other that escape begins to seem as impossible as happiness. The attraction is considerable; so is the damage. The song previews Infinite Fountain, Night Nail’s fourth studio album, due November 6, 2026, through Icy Cold Records. Its accompanying video reunites the band with director and editor Jean De Oliviera, whose previous collaborations include Hollow Day, Little Armenia, and Narcoleptic Dream Catcher. Vile Train begins with a noise suspended somewhere between a buzz and a screech, while cold guitar tones gather around it with considerable menace. The drums establish their footing before a heavier, sustained riff saws through the opening, its melody making the abrasion strangely inviting. Around the thirty-second mark, the bass enters with a deep, brooding groove, and the guitar shifts into a lower, more resonant register. That change gives the song a mournful richness, setting the scene for Brandon Robert’s dark, swaggering delivery. Repeating synth figures tighten the tension beneath his voice, and roughly a minute in, the chorus sends the arrangement into a more urgent gothic dance beat. The construction is remarkably assured: each entrance increases the pressure, while the bass keeps enough melodic independence to make the groove feel alive. By the three-minute mark, its intricate phrasing has become a hook in its own right, moving beneath Robert’s breathy repetition of “Daydreams and nightmares” as a feminine voice echoes the words in whispers. The song’s pleasure comes from those relationships between the instruments, the way an ominous opening develops into something so physically persuasive. Robert found the initial inspiration during a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested a romance with a particularly poor prognosis. In the song’s conception, two dreamers inhabit separate modern realities until their fantasies bring them together. They exchange clothes, cigarettes, and intimacies, gradually making a prison of the connection that first seemed to offer freedom. Robert describes the result as “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The lyrics give that deterioration a nasty intimacy. Caution sits beside fawning, attraction beside aggression, and the lovers seem increasingly aware of the roles they have been playing. “Some days I wish I was her” carries the confusion further, towards the point where wanting another person begins to erase the distinction between their identity and your own. Against the recurring admission of lies, the fantasy of America offers another possible elsewhere. Every imagined exit seems to lead back to the same two people. Vile Train was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. That combination serves a song whose writing and arrangement make its gothic excess feel earned, with a chorus capable of turning private misery into a crowded dance floor. Directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera, the video gives Vile Train a stark black-and-white treatment, cutting between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor shots framed by stone arches and fountain basins. Black leather, dark glasses, and severe makeup give the pair a suitably funereal glamour, while tight shots of fingers on strings bring the song’s instrumental interplay into focus. Robert’s face repeatedly fills the frame, his dark lipstick and pale features isolated against the black background. Grain, scratches, and superimposed silhouettes of reaching hands disturb that severe simplicity, spreading across faces and instruments until the musicians seem caught behind the image itself. Robert’s own gestures towards the lens make the camera feel uncomfortably close, turning performance into something between an invitation and an accusation. The recurring close-ups and grasping hands give the song’s obsession a physical form, suggesting an intimacy that has become impossible to escape. It is an effective visual rendering of what the band calls the “afterlife of relationship hell,” where the desire to hold someone close has acquired a distinctly claustrophobic meaning. Watch the video for Vile Train below: Formed in Los Angeles in 2013, Night Nail relocated to Berlin in 2018, the year their debut album LA Demons appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed through Cold Transmission in 2020, with Fates Explained arriving on Metropolis Records in 2023. The archival release Early Demons and Demos and remix album Fates Remade followed in 2024. Their earlier work with producer Pete Burns of Kill Shelter helped establish a catalogue that connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes. Infinite Fountain also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the album with shows across the US, UK, and Europe during 2026–2027. In the meantime, explore their back catalog on Bandcamp. items.album: Faded Pulse Finds Solace in the Past on Ethereal Goth Album “Elysia”
items.excerpt: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain.
