items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的新专辑延续了她一贯模糊而难以归类的音乐语言，将民谣根基、前卫即兴与宗教仪式感融为一体。中提琴、手风琴、击弦古钢琴与钢琴构成核心编制，本作加入鼓、贝斯与合成器，拓宽了声场维度。大量作品采用一遍即兴录制完成，营造出穿越时间的静谧神秘感，如约翰·克莱尔诗作改编的曲目在持续低音之上承载超脱旋律。多首曲目带有中世纪圣咏的影子，缓慢级进的钢琴线条成为专辑的情感锚点。整张专辑也是对亡父的纪念，丧失感渗透于音符之间，特别是描写父亲最后一次造访自留地的挽歌式作品。光明与暗影在音乐中交融渗透，情绪不断转换，作品拒绝被简单归类，融合民俗素材与现代即兴手法，最终形成只属于 Cotton 本人的独特声响世界。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 本合辑聚焦贝宁乐手Antoine Dougb与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo于1977至1982年的合作录音，由专注于非洲及热带音乐的独立厂牌Analog Africa发行。Dougbe以拍击大腿演绎Cavacha节奏著称，该节奏源于鼓手Belobi Meridjo对火车节拍的提炼，后广泛渗透至七十年代中期的刚果流行乐。Dougbe身为伏都教实践者，对合作乐手要求严苛，认为唯有Poly-Rythmo能精准实现其构想。其录音生涯虽短暂，仅三张专辑与数支单曲，但展现出强劲的创作能量。音乐根植于伏都教仪式传统，融合Sato与Sakpata律动，吉他音色带有时代特有的塑料光泽，合成器开始渗入编制。古巴son的影响在前几首尤为明显，《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器铺底，闪烁吉他与高帽主导的律动交织；《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》则更为直接地呈现古巴元素，包括持续牛铃与鼻音应答唱法。整体呈现西非节奏传统与古巴、刚果流行的跨文化对话。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: Space Afrika 是来自曼彻斯特的二人组合，这张《Quiet Storm》相较前作在编制上大幅扩展，引入弦乐、竖琴以及多位客席乐人。乐评以雨后阳光来临前那种灰金色的独特光线作为贯穿全文的意象，形容他们的音乐始终栖居于这种暧昧的过渡时刻。前作以短波收音机的低语、塔楼间的风声为特征，传递身处人群却全然孤寂的氛围；新作在此基础上将音色边界进一步推开，融合原声乐器与电子处理，形成更为丰富的层次感。文章作为乐评序章尚未深入展开具体曲目的技术分析，但已点明这是一次从极简环境声响向多层次融合美学的跨越，对实验电子与氛围音乐的听众具有吸引力。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A surprisingly-sophisticated and highly-entertaining album from a group of University of Illinois college students! Released on Brunswick Records in July of 1972.1. "The Monster Bride" (10:36) a very proggy, early King Crimson and Yes-like opening of bass, organ, clarinet, and delicate cymbal play turns in the second minute toward proggy brass rock--more like ELP meets BS&T. In the third minute the motif starts to smooth out before suddenly switching direction toward more light and playful circus music and then, in the fourth minute there is an equally sudden directional change toward more avant/eclectic Jazz-Rock Fusion before going Crimson and Zappa in the fifth. This is all quite tightly-performed and very sophisticated and unpredictable! It must have been something to compose and then pull off as a band in 1970s studio conditions. By the time we get to the end of the sixth minute everything slows down to a cymbal-supported droning organ for a Peter Hammill-like male vocal to enter and sing. Very Crimsonian! Flute and piano pick up from here with a very pretty, almost CHICAGO-like melody presentation and passage which builds and builds, horns entering and gathering forces over bass, guitar, and drum's rhythm track. At 5:22 everything stops for some percussion-backed dramatic very theatric narration of a sexually-piqued scene of the monster's reaction and response to the birth of his bride and child--which then leads to a finishing burst of CHICAGO-like brass rock. Very interesting! The sophistication of the compositions (and ability to pull it off in the studio) is the most impressive part. (18.375/20) 2. "Spiders (In Neals Basement)" (5:57) an accented male voice singing a sly lyric of film noir's detective-type music, like musical themes for scenes in a New Orleans juke joint or Chicago flop house. The music, performances both instrumentally and vocally are so colorful and spry. Great brassy theater music and great entertainment! Amazing that these were just a bunch of college kids! (9.333/10)3. "Witches Theme And Dance" (9:47) a brass rock song that opens like a LIGHTHOUSE song with great pace and energy before dropping down into a slow, plodding motif over which the gang issue some great four-part vocal harmony vocals. These guys must've done music theater or high school theater music. Bassist Neal Rosner is quite impressive (and, thankfully, placed forward in the mix), sounding a lot like Goblin or PFM's bassists. More stunning theatric stop-and-start composition performed with ease and professional precision over/within which electric guitar, voices, slide flute, and other mildly scary Hallowe'en noises contribute their solos and incidentals. Nice trilly flute solo in the final third--augmented by awesome "distant" flugelhorn. The finish is just perfect for the "lesson" of the witchy allegory. Another gem of a song; these guys are so creative and so talented! (18.875/20)4. "A Brief Message From Your Local Media" (9:59) here the band conjures up a four-part suite. It opens sounding like something from Aaron Copeland before organ, bass, hi-hat & bass drum lay down a soft carpet for a lone vocalist to begin his GREG LAKE-like "In the Court of the Crimson King" imitation. Obligatory flute joins in as "Greg" reaches his third verse--arpeggiated guitar chords and increasingly MICHAEL GILES-like drumming, as well. Around 4:30 there is a break in which narrator delivers a brief spoken-word summation of the contributions of Henry Ford to the workings of modern society, which is then followed by the development of a new motif of rather up-tempo organ- and flute-driven Jazz-Rock--which gains Latin elements in the eighth minute to give it a LEONARD BERNSTEIN West Side Story feel but then about a minute later the music moves more toward a pop/theatric-Brass Rock form similar to the snarky Hair, Godspel, and Pippen phenomenons. The music ends with a fading out calliope and military drums sound. Interesting. Though still delightfully creative and astonishingly sophisticated, the cohesiveness of this one is questionable (but, then, so is the flow of the typical radio or television programming!). (18.125/20) - a) "The Garden"- b) "The Assembly Line"- c) "Electric Man"- d) "Question"Total time 36:19Jazzy, brassy Crimsonian prog rock that sounds quite mature for a bunch of Illini students--and it's so entertaining, even addictive! Incredible for a debut album.A/five stars; a surprisingly-sophisticated and well-polished display of delightfully-entertaining compositions and performances. Who knew?! And, Whatever happened to?

items.body: Columbus’s Pinta, Niña and Santa María sail through “Delfín del Mundo” alongside pineapples, cockerels, chocolate, tobacco and caipirinhas, a roll call of conquest and tropical produce chanted over a psychedelic cumbia. “Delfín del Mundo” is the third and final single from Desertropical, the new EP from Dr. Rayo, due in October on Costa Rican label Lácteo Cósmico. The project belongs to Red Jesus, a Chilean-Mexican percussionist and producer who spent 2014 to 2020 on Mexico’s independent circuit. Now based in Madrid, he launched the project with a sold-out night at Moby Dick. Red Jesus made the track with Barzo, the San José-born DJ and producer who runs Lácteo Cósmico and has remixed Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu. He came to Madrid for a short visit, and the pair recorded most of the instruments live at Dr. Rayo’s base. Barzo then built the electronic production on top of those takes. The earlier singles “Mexicali Tropical” and “Owl on Cocaine” opened big and dramatic, while “Delfín del Mundo” settles into a mid-tempo sway built on a slow-burning bassline, live percussion and a vocal delivered close to a chant. The vocal carries a message of pride in Latin American roots, and the cacao, tobacco and pineapples in the lyric were growing in the Americas long before Columbus’s ships arrived. Desertropical gets a launch party at Madrid’s Siroco at the end of September, with Spanish dates to follow in Seville, Oviedo, Gijón, Logroño and Santander. Stream “Delfín del Mundo” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Dr. Rayo x Barzo – Delfín del Mundo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Rysiek P. — An opportunity like this certainly cannot be overlooked. Twenty years after releasing their debut album, *Armed Forces of Simantipak*, the band Khatsaturjan?whose name derives from the renowned Armenian composer Aram Khachaturian?has released a new record titled *Monolog Chronosa*. Their discography also includes two other albums - *Disconcerto Grosso* (2010) and *Beast, Machine & Man* (2015) - and their history is notable for the fact that, as early as their 2002 debut single *Aramsome Sums*, they performed their own "rock" versions of Modest Mussorgsky's *Night on Bald Mountain* and Hector Berlioz's *March to the Scaffold*. All of this was presented in progressive hard-rock arrangements that incorporated elements reminiscent of the band Gentle Giant. Furthermore, critics hailed the group's first album as a benchmark for symphonic rock. One might pessimistically remark, "But that was years ago". Yet, it is certainly worth checking out where Khatsaturjan stands today. The band's latest release comprises forty-seven minutes of music spread across seven tracks, with an album title suggesting that the passage of time is the central theme. This phenomenon is observed and described from various perspectives - including, perhaps most importantly, the human condition and the personal, often highly subjective experience of life passing by. The title of the opening track - "Lessons (On Human Obsolescence)" - gives one food for thought right from the start. However, do not expect dark, atmospheric arrangements here. The composition is remarkably balanced,almost conservative in its playing style and employs familiar progressive rock tropes, with one notable exception: a strong emphasis on vocal polyphony (a true hallmark of this album) and a more prominent role for keyboards. These two elements define the musical structure of the song, which opens with the sound of a bell before embarking on a progressive journey rich in engaging tempo shifts and instrumental virtuosity. The second track, "What Was True," takes a slightly different approach. Here, the band clearly leans toward a modern progressive sound, successfully utilizing "new textures" to craft a unique atmosphere that straddles the line between atmospheric progressive rock (or even neo-prog) and a vocal-harmony-driven ballad. Once again, vocal polyphony and synthesizers serve as the building blocks for both this specific track and the album as a whole. The track "The Dystopian Spirit Of Club Energy" also features a piano-and-synthesizer-driven sound. Yet, in this composition, the band draws upon classical music and classical time signatures. The piano sets the arrangement's course, serving as a backdrop for highly impressive vocal performances. Only halfway through does the track remind us that it is 2026, showing how a guitar-driven rhythmic boost can yield a truly successful result. Incorporating electronic elements into the arrangement only enhances the musical value of this piece, which runs over five minutes in length. It was only while listening to "Song Of Days" that I realized what truly draws me to the band's music: a delicacy and almost theatrical storytelling style, skillfully blended with classical influences, alongside magnificent tales sung with a masterful, gradual build-up of vocal intensity. With a full arsenal of musical tools at their disposal, Khatsaturjan selects only those that fit the symphonic-progressive narrative, all while keeping classical music traditions close at hand. "Song Of Days" is a perfect example of this approach. It makes brilliant use of symphonic arrangements, blending them with flawless vocal lines and weaving in thoroughly modern progressive guitar motifs to create a truly well-crafted track. "DID Memoir" shares a similar, song-oriented character. It opens with a "classic" sense of grandeur, progressive guitar work, and... such delicate vocals. Everything weaves together into a structure that challenges the listener - filled with improvisational passages that hark back to classical music and, as an added bonus, theatrical farce-style interludes appearing midway through the fourth minute. Just listen closely around the five-minute mark for a dose of rap; this element, yet another instance of the piece's stylistic multiplicity, is entirely justified given the title: "DID Memoir." While the acronym refers to Dissociative Identity Disorder, it also serves as a fitting title for the track's eclectic, multi-stylistic nature. Following a symphonic opening, the penultimate track on this magnificent album - "The Keepers of the Philosopher's Stone" - simply sends shivers down the spine with its superb vocal lines. It features backing vocals, humming passages, and a lead vocal that stands out tonally, its rough timbre lending an air of deep mystery. Yet, what makes this composition truly exceptional is the extensive and successful incorporation of motifs drawn from classical music; the violin sounds and classical time signatures transform this five-plus-minute piece into a remarkable puzzle of motifs and an intricate arrangement. A madrigal-like character, blended with thoroughly modern synthesizer and guitar sounds, seems to elevate the track's central theme - fittingly so for a song about the "Philosopher's Stone," which here truly transmutes individual notes into "gold." With this release, the end comes all too soon. Were it not for the fact that the closing track - "Mundus Meus (This World of Mine)" - employs every possible device to captivate the listener from the very first note, one might feel that the magnificent preceding track left something musically unresolved, a void that could neither be filled nor replaced. "Mundus Meus..." stands as a magnificent anthem and the perfect culmination of the album; the Latin lyrics sound both prophetic and majestic without detracting from the depth of the message. And although the track features numerous gentle prog-metal solos, it remains, at its core, a thoroughly symphonic-progressive composition. If I say that I am very - truly very - pleasantly surprised by the latest work from the group Khatsaturjan, is that recommendation enough? If not, I'll add that the band features essentially the same lineup as on their debut and subsequent albums, even though musical light-years have passed since that first release (in 2002). Atte Kurri (vocals, bass, keyboards), Ilkka Piispala (vocals, drums, keyboards, bass), and Ilkka Saarikivi (vocals, keyboards, bass, violin) continue to demonstrate that musical trends don't matter to them. It is significant that Khatsaturjan is a group of friends who get together only when they want to record something; they are not a band that makes a living from touring and recording albums. On their Facebook page, the band writes: "We work slowly because Khatsaturjan is not our profession - it is a passion project and a beloved hobby. Whenever we decide to work on a new album, we know a years-long effort lies ahead, with no financial reward whatsoever. Yet, time and again, we take on new projects." Perhaps this approach allows them to maintain a sense of detachment and find the tranquility needed to create new music? You surely know that things tend to flow more easily when there are no deadlines hanging over your head. And since we will likely have to wait a long time for the next sign of musical life from Khatsaturjan, we should simply enjoy this highly successful release - one that has earned a spot in my top ten albums of the year.

items._cn_summary: 亚美尼亚乐队KHATSATURJAN暌违二十年推出新作，以《时间老人的独白》探讨时间流逝与人类境况。专辑共七首曲目，总长四十七分钟，以多元视角审视时间这一核心主题。编曲以声部复调与键盘为两大支柱，开场曲以钟声引入，节奏变换频繁且器乐炫技。第二曲偏向新派前卫质感，融合氛围化音色与人声和声。另一首曲目以钢琴与合成器驱动，融入古典音乐语汇与复杂节拍，中段引入吉他节奏推进，并辅以电子元素增强层次。整体风格在前卫摇滚框架内融入古典元素与复调人声，兼具传统与现代审美，是一支具有东欧文化背景的交响前卫乐队的新作。

items.body: Adrian Utley, the guitarist and co-founder of Portishead, has reworked “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” from Polish composer Mariusz Szypura’s “Chopin Residue,” a project that removes the piano entirely from nine of Frédéric Chopin’s best-known piano pieces. The rework arrives today as the latest single from the double album, which Cleopatra Records brings to CD and double vinyl on 16 October; an immersive Blu-ray edition mixed in Dolby Atmos is already available. Chopin Residue by Mariusz Szypura Szypura said working with Utley was a long-held ambition: “Adrian and Portishead are among my favourite musicians. The sound, the approach to making music, the search for unobvious and lo-fi textures, all of it had an enormous influence on me.” Szypura kept the harmonic structure and phrasing of Chopin’s originals while stripping out the instrument itself. He described the decision as a matter of respect rather than provocation: “I rejected the piano immediately. […] I decided Chopin didn’t deserve such profanation. I could only approach this material through the prism of my own sensitivity, harmony, and deconstruction. So I took the piano out. […] The piano was the delivery system, not the content.” Adrian Utley’s rework of ‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ “Chopin Residue” splits into two discs: “Deconstructions,” on which Szypura rebuilds nine Chopin pieces with a cast including Lee Ranaldo (Sonic Youth), David Pajo (Slint), Joey Waronker, Gail Ann Dorsey, John McEntire (Tortoise) and John Stanier (Battles), and “Reworks,” on which a second group of artists takes those deconstructed recordings further from the source. Utley’s “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” opens the second disc alongside reworks by Fennesz, Matthew Herbert, Masayoshi Fujita, Sean O’Hagan, Jim O’Rourke, Christine Ott, Benoît Pioulard and Abul Mogard. Szypura described the difference between the two discs directly: “‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ is Adrian’s reconstruction, not my piece with his guitar on top. That is the principle of the whole second disc: nine artists, nine rebuilds, each in their own language.” The two discs are designed to be played together as well as separately, an idea that extends into the Blu-ray edition’s Dolby Atmos mix. Szypura said: “They were built to overlap. […] In stereo you hear an arrangement. In Atmos you’re inside the harmonic space with the piano missing from the middle of it. […] That’s not a format upgrade, it’s closer to what the piece was always trying to do.” “Chopin Residue” gets its UK stage premiere at London’s Cadogan Hall on 26 September, as part of the Polish Jazz Festival. Its packaging has also picked up a Bronze A’ Design Award and a Red Dot Award. About Adrian Utley and Mariusz Szypura Adrian Utley was born in Northampton in 1957 and moved to Bristol in the mid-1980s, where he played guitar in touring bands led by jazz organist Big John Patton and drummer Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers. He co-founded Portishead in Bristol in 1991 with Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons, co-producing and playing on the band’s albums “Dummy” (1994), “Portishead” (1997) and “Third” (2008). Outside the band, Utley has recorded and toured with Marianne Faithfull, Jeff Beck and Will Gregory of Goldfrapp, leads his own ensemble Adrian Utley’s Guitar Orchestra, and has scored film and audio work with director Nic Roeg, naturalist David Attenborough and Britain’s National Trust. Mariusz Szypura is a composer, producer and visual artist born in 1972 and based in Warsaw. He started out in the early 1990s in the Poznań rock band Happy Pills before founding his main recording project, Silver Rocket, releasing five albums including “Infinity Fidelity,” a Dolby Atmos record that won Gold for Music/Film Cover at the 2025 European Design Awards. His installation work includes “in:human” at the Centre for Contemporary Art Ujazdowski Castle in Warsaw (2024) and “êkhos” at Lincoln Center during Unsound Festival New York (2024). “Chopin Residue” grew out of that installation practice: Szypura first released the album digitally and on 2LP, 2CD, 2MC and Blu-ray through his own Black Element Label in Warsaw on 28 November 2025, alongside gallery and listening events in New York, Osaka, Los Angeles and Warsaw. Cleopatra Records now extends that release internationally, bringing “Chopin Residue” to CD and double vinyl on 16 October 2026 while the Blu-ray Immersive Edition remains available from its earlier release.

items.body: Stabbing Westward Wither – ReWired COP International Re-recording a classic album is a risky proposition for any band or artist. Even leaving aside the shady practice of creating soundalike recordings to get in on streaming and sync royalties, the upside of recreating your own work is dubious; technically better performances, recording or production isn’t an improvement when a classic LP’s appeal is in familiarity, shortcomings and all. The best case scenario is that you come up with an interesting alternate take on your own material, but the more common outcome is sounding like a cover band. Thankfully, in the case of Stabbing Westward’s Wither – ReWired, a completely new version of the band’s 1996 breakthrough sophomore album Wither, Blister, Burn + Peel, the band have taken an approach that justifies the endeavor. Signed during the industrial rock’s brief moment of mainstream relevance in the 90s, the original record had catchy songs and benefited hugely from frontman Christopher Hall’s oh-so dramatic alt-rock vocals, but notably buried the majority of the band’s electronic elements beneath mountains of guitar chug. Wither – ReWired addresses that in a way that merely doing a new mix of the original tapes (if that were even an option) couldn’t, by not just recreating, but fully rearranging the songs to give the programming and synthwork equal billing. The results are striking in an A to B comparison of each version. Tracks that felt like lesser moments such as opener “I Don’t Believe” and “Crushing Me” are given a whole new life, the former by wedding a strong programmed rhythm section to the proceedings, the latter by upping the tempo and dialing back the original’s turgid guitars in favour of a sharp, forward moving arrangement. In the case of the record’s best and most memorable moments, such as the rock radio hit “What Do I Have to Do?”, things are left well enough alone, with minor tweaks to programming and the mix to keep it consistent with the rest of the record’s sound. In fact, they stick so close to how you expect those cuts to sound that the small changes stick out; Hall changes some of his vocal phrasing on the chorus to “Shame” in a way that feels wrong at first, but becomes comfortable after a few listens. The other important aspect of Wither – ReWired is in how its songs are sequenced as a listening experience. Where the 1996 original frontloads the record’s singles and most commercial cuts, the new version places songs in an order that feels like it makes more sense. “Slipping Away” is moved from the closing spot, its new club-ready iteration placed to pick things up from the mid-tempo melodrama of “Why?”, replaced by a revamped version of B-side “Agekata (Dawn)” whose more atmospheric synth textures better fit the role. “So Wrong” and “Inside You” (a deep cut that is secretly one of the band’s best moments) have significant time shaved off and are placed to keep the momentum and emotion of the record up leading into the final third. The amount of effort into making a genuinely new, but not unfamiliar album are considerable, and act as evidence that this is anything but a cash-in. Stabbing Westward could have churned out a quick and dirty version of their live set in studio and called it a day, but instead Wither ReWired is a genuinely considered undertaking by a band who understand who they were, who they are, and how to reconcile the thirty year gap in those incarnations. Buy it. Wither – ReWired by Stabbing Westward The post Stabbing Westward, “Wither – ReWired” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: As you are likely well aware, this week marks the 100th anniversary of John Coltrane's birth and writers and friends of the Free Jazz Blog were asked to contribute their personal thoughts on his music and influence. The parameters for the contributions were loose, only that it should be something personal and if it so happened that an album appeared more than once, that was fine, as what it meant to the writer was surely different. We ended up with our biggest feature ever! For the next two weeks we will be featuring reflections, reviews, and anecdotes about Coltrane and his groundbreaking music. We begin today an introduction from Sammy Stein. Enjoy! Paul Acquaro John Coltrane. Src: wikipedia By Sammy Stein FJC is celebrating John Coltrane’s 100 th year. For anyone unfamiliar with his music, the following offers a brief overview of why Coltrane is ranked amongst the greatest of musicians. Through his approach, style, delivery, and unmistakable sound, Coltrane powered through the door that Ornette Coleman and others had left ajar, revealing jazz’s powerful, emotive, and transformational heart. Nothing post-Coltrane is untouched by his influence. His was not a deliberate subversion of traditional jazz, but an uncalculated stream of events, personal, spiritual, and historical, that converged in a confluence that formed his music. Coltrane’s mother bought him a saxophone when he was sixteen, and he was influenced by players including Illinois Jacquet. His grandparents were ordained ministers, his parents met through the church, and Coltrane grew up influenced by religion. He chose a different path – that of music and was not discouraged by family, yet later in his life, it was God who helped him save his music and career. Without his spiritual reawakening, Coltrane’s career may have faded. Early on, he was supported by musicians who recognised his prodigious talent. However, he became addicted to drugs and would arrive for gigs unshaven and in smelly, wrinkled clothes. He might fall asleep on stage. Miles Davis fired him, and Dizzy Gillespie didn’t follow suit only because of their friendship and his respect for Coltrane’s talent. At the nadir of his life, Coltrane reached out to God. He described a revelation he had when God spoke to him, and he set about composing exquisite music, praising God and teaching his followers. He said, “My goal is to live the truly religious life and express it through my music. If you can live it, there’s no problem about the music, because it’s part of the whole thing.” Coltrane’s first wife, Naima, was central to his early spiritual journey. A practicing Muslim, she helped him understand God’s presence in their lives. With her support, he overcame addiction within a year. His second wife, Alice, became his spiritual partner and musical collaborator. A pianist and harpist, she understood Coltrane’s desire to contribute to a greater purpose through music. Some of Coltrane’s music has an intangible quality. He understood the spiritual and temporal worlds, and his music fused the two, expressing deep spiritual inquiry alongside the mortal complexities of personality. Jazz became a place where the human condition could be expressed with unflinching honesty and transcendent beauty. Coltrane was playing at a time when conditions were ripe for rebellion and change, and he was profoundly affected by events of his time, especially the civil rights movement, initially siding with Malcolm X before aligning with Martin Luther King Jr’s belief in peaceful but persistent protest. He performed eight benefit concerts to support Martin Luther King Jr’s cause. His music channeled anger at racism and discrimination, despair at humanity’s darkness, and the beauty of praise and worship. He had faced the demons of addiction and won, and his music reflected beauty, was personal yet spoke to millions. The murder of four African American girls in the KKK bombing in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963 profoundly affected Coltrane. Two months after the event, he took McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones into Rudy Van Gelder's studio and recorded ‘Alabama’, later released on the album Live At Birdland (Impulse 1964). As discontent rose, Coltrane’s modal technique challenged preconceived ideas about traditional jazz. Under his and other musicians’ tenure, jazz, ever the mirror of society, became more dissonant and unruly. Coltrane’s music is as relevant today as it was in the 1960s. The messages are clearly and profoundly expressed and cut to the core impulses of humanity. Because of his uncloaked humanity, listening to Coltrane feels as emergent and alive for someone encountering the music today as it did to listeners forty years, or ten years ago. Coltrane’s near-mythical status was helped by the Blue Note label, which signed Coltrane and other players, seen as risky at the time, and some iconic images, notably photographs by Francis Wolff, a skilled photographer and executive of Blue Note. Of over 33,000 pictures Wolff took (probably more), his images of John Coltrane in moments of intense concentration or creativity seem to capture the musician's essence. One of Coltrane’s gifts was his ability to perform as a soloist or as part of an ensemble. Pieces like Davis’s’ ‘Milestones’ with ‘Cannonball’ Adderley (alto sax) and Coltrane (tenor sax) responding to Davis’s trumpet with twists and turns within the original mode laid a template for modal playing (try also Coltrane's’ Spiral’ and ‘Naima’ from Giant Steps (Atlantic 1959)). Modal jazz led away from traditional jazz and toward free jazz. Free playing was where Coltrane was headed. In the 1960s, some journalists described early free jazz as a poison to jazz, and Downbeat critics described Coltrane and Dolphy’s playing as ‘nihilistic exercises’ and ‘anti-jazz.’ Miles Davis found free jazz difficult to embrace initially. However, a few years later Davis, like Coltrane and others, found free jazz liberating. Coltrane, like many free-playing musicians, connected the evolution of the music with a deepening of self-realization and the strengthening and expression of their beliefs. Alongside fellow musicians Yusef Lateef, Sonny Rollins, and others, Coltrane pursued musical mastery and self-realization. In his suite A Love Supreme (Impulse, 1965), Coltrane expressed his love and awe of God, and the final movement is based on a devotional poem he wrote. He studied different religions and philosophies, including the Indian philosophy of Jiddu Krishnamurti, which he was introduced to by Bill Evans. Coltrane perhaps expressed his love for God most during his free playing. His tracks ‘Love’ and ‘The Father, And The Son And the Holy Ghost’ on Meditations (Impulse 1965), albums Ascension (Impulse 1966), Om (Impulse, recorded 1965, released 1966), and ‘Peace on Earth’ from Infinity (Impulse, recorded 1966, released 1972), reflect his beliefs. Coltrane used the ferocity of his playing and complex techniques as a way of worship. He said he created music for God and others and wanted to be the opposing force to evil. Even those unaware of his driving beliefs find something special, untouchable, and unique in his music. Coltrane, Art Blakey, Yusef Lateef, and other musicians became part of the Ahmadiyya sect of Islam, which forbids the intake of drugs and alcohol. Coltrane said, "My music is the spiritual expression of what I am - my faith, my knowledge, my being. When you begin to see the possibilities of music, you desire to do something really good for people, to help humanity free itself from its hang-ups…I want to speak to their souls.” Some found Coltrane’s later music, with its contradictions and unresolved transitions, less pure than his earlier recordings, but for many, they remain some of the best work produced by any jazz musician. Two weeks before his death, Coltrane discussed opening a music venue without alcohol as he realized this had masked his creativity. After Coltrane died in 1967, aged just forty, Alice kept pushing musical boundaries, and her music took on a profoundly spiritual element. She collaborated with Ornette Coleman, Pharoah Sanders, and many others, and her music traversed from blues-infused melodies to unfathomable sonic journeys, but it was beautiful, and her talent won armies of devotees, so, partly through Alice, Coltrane’s legacy remained. Also through his sons. John Jr, Ravi, and Oranyan. Oranyan started playing jazz with his brothers but has gone into trance and electronic music production. John Jr was a promising bassist but was killed in a car accident when he was 17, and Ravi is a jazz musician. Alice’s grandnephew, Steven Ellison, AKA Flying Lotus, is a record label owner, producer, rapper, and DJ. Many of his recordings feature jazz samples. Coltrane’s music and persona continue to influence music and musicians. From those who followed directly, including Pharoah Sanders, Lonnie Liston, Sun Ra, Don Cherry, and John McLaughlin, to nearly every jazz musician today. In 2016,’ Alabama’ was included in John DeJohnette's 2016 album In Movement (ECM), and on this recording, sons of the original artists, including saxophonist Ravi Coltrane (son of Coltrane) and bassist Matthew Garrison (son of bassist Jimmy Garrison), played. Coltrane’s music has been sampled on recordings by hip hop artists, younger jazz musicians, and many others. FJC is celebrating the fact that Coltrane left his influence, and there are some great pieces following this introduction. It is impossible to adequately record the influence of John Coltrane on the music that followed, but we can try. As a jazz musician recently said to me, ‘Don’t worry, just stick on some ‘Trane.” Perhaps more than any other jazz musician, John Coltrane showed there is a way to play from the heart without constraints. When you can do that, you allow your true spirit to reveal itself. Like ‘Trane. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 为纪念约翰·柯川诞辰一百周年，多位撰稿人分享了各自对其音乐的个人感受与影响。文章以萨米·斯泰因的引言开篇，概述了柯川作为爵士先驱的地位，指出他推开了奥尔尼·科尔曼等人半开的门，揭示了爵士乐充满力量、情感与蜕变的核心。文章回顾了柯川的生平：十六岁接触萨克斯、教会家庭的熏陶、成名早期的毒瘾危机、被迈尔斯·戴维斯解雇的经历，以及随后通过宗教觉醒实现的精神与音乐重生。文中还谈及他与两任妻子奈玛与艾丽斯的关系，前者帮助他戒除毒瘾，后者则成为他音乐与精神上的合作伙伴。文章强调了柯川音乐中难以言喻的精神性，并引用他的话说明其创作目标是过真正虔诚的生活并通过音乐表达信仰。整体为纪念性介绍，未深入具体专辑的音响细节或曲目分析。

items.body: As Solid opens its gates, the music takes a single step forward before lifting off. A nascent, endlessly-echoing piano joins a grounded bass – the only part of the music that touches the ground at all – and an airy, washed-out progression enters, too, blossoming into something like a spring breeze. Swirling in light, yogurt-like textures and a playground spirit, sustaining itself and imbued with a fulfilling light, ‘Stones’ is the kindest of openers from Poland’s ambient duo, Bojanek & Michalowski. Things open up even more as the music begins to shape itself, resembling something like a mystical temple which reveals itself to only a select few. The electric guitar bends the atmosphere, shaping it by way of sonic architecture into a towering figure composed out of monolithic distortion and frayed melodies; a statue carving out the face of a God. The guitar rises slowly, gaining momentum as a rolling wave will as it approaches the shore before reaching the point of no return. It then breaks itself, collapsing like the dusty, sand-strewn stone that it is, an ancient rock that can no longer stand. This is where the track’s power lies: in its breaking. The distortion climbs, morphing into the indiscernible roaring of insectile static. It both washes and stains. The music rises up to titanic heights, and this is indicative of the track naming – monoliths, pillars, statues, sculptures. Even the greatest masterpiece must begin with a single stroke, and each journey must begin with a single step. Likewise, the opening note is the alpha and the omega, the first stone at the base of this perfectly-aligned pyramid; habitually repeating, but turning silence into sound and a Sahara drought into an overflowing oasis. At some level, the music is burning in a spell of torturous heat. Temperature-wise,Solid summons up the merciless spike of July or August, but it’s a dry heat, and not a humid, shirt-sticking suffocation. These pillars stand tall and proud. Even during the clashing of tribal drums, the music remains ambient and expansive enough, despite the dog-lead of repetition. But it acts both ways: one person may think of the bass as a restraint, but the bassline can also be a guide, a map back to camp via the predictability of its looping phrase. Popular music is built on anticipation, but it exists in ambient, too – usually in the form of traditional song, with examples being the vocal-heavy music of Julianna Barwick or Alicia Merz. This anticipation and release, this question and answer, can also be found in a loop, albeit lacking a proper resolution because of its repetition. Solid is energetic ambient, the kind that makes you feel alive instead of dosing it up on sleeping pills. Altitude is everywhere in the record. The flight attendant on ‘Figures’ asks passengers to put their seat belts on as the descent begins, but the reverb-soaked, cloud-wispy guitar chords are more like fluttering feathers or falling autumn leaves after the death of summer, while Jacaszek’s remix glides through cut-up pads and skimmers over soft and thin beats. Have a nice flight… www.ncoded.pl

items._cn_summary: 波兰双人组Bojanek & Michalowski的专辑《Solid》以氛围音乐为基底，融合电吉他回授、循环贝斯线与部落鼓点，构建出从寂静到轰鸣的渐进式音景。乐评将开篇曲比作神殿石柱的雕塑过程，单音逐步堆叠至失真巨浪，最终崩解为昆虫般的静态噪音。整张专辑被描述为充满海拔感与干燥热度的'有能量的氛围音乐'，与Julianna Barwick等人声氛围传统形成呼应，强调loop结构中的期待与释放机制。评论指出贝斯既是束缚也是引导线索，重复在重复中完成了对寂静与干旱的转化。整体文本在氛围音乐的美学描述上较为诗意，但对具体声音设计细节着墨有限。

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以墨西哥牛仔文化与夏威夷的历史交汇为线索，将西班牙语和夏威夷语歌曲以互相翻译歌词的方式重新编排，融合尤克里里、墨西哥竖琴、手风琴及滑棒吉他等乐器，形成跨文化的民谣合集。专辑在加州一间录音室五天内完成，以同期录音为主，邀请了Taj Mahal、David Hidalgo等资深音乐人参与，并纳入学院学生的演奏，呈现真实的现场感和即兴扩展。曲目涵盖传统夏威夷民歌、墨西哥老歌新编以及原创作品，Woody Guthrie的《Deportee》被改编为带有社会评论色彩的版本，凸显移民劳工议题。整体编排密集而统一，既尊重两地的音乐传统，也展现了语言、世代之间的合作精神。

David Dzubinski
as part of the
Prism Quartet
's new series of collaborations called
Unlocking Your Inner Composer
. If you have listened to my radio programs, you are probably familiar with the quartet's ground-breaking, genre-blurring music. If not, there's no better introduction than this.

Ursula Rucker

Tyshawn Sorey

Carlos Santiago

items._cn_summary: 这首由作曲家Dzubinski创作的作品由Prism四重奏联合人声、打击乐与小提琴共同演绎，属于该四重奏"解锁你的内在作曲家"系列合作项目之一。演出于2025年11月在费城自由图书馆完成，时长不到四分钟，从原始粗砺到抒情流畅再回到原点，展现出短小精悍的结构控制力。评论仅以三句话概括感受，未深入分析作曲技法或表演细节。人声、打击乐和弦乐的三角配置暗示了跨界对话的意图，但文章本身缺少对实验性或即兴成分的具体描述，信息量有限。对于关注实验爵士与当代古典交叉领域的听众，这是一次值得关注的小型现场演出，但其媒体呈现较为简略。

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items._cn_summary: 丹麦三人组合 GuldGanger 的首张数字 EP，由北欧民谣界资深主唱 Mia Guldhammer 领衔。五首作品大多取材自传统素材，乐队成员各自带来不同诠释，嗓音苍劲古朴。开场曲《Svennedal》节奏粗犷奔弛，充分展现主唱说服力十足的声线；《Nordgård》以口簧琴和风笛推动律动，是唯一一首由乐队成员 Morten Musicus 创作的原创作品。传统曲目《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》融入扬琴作为细腻底色，终曲《Ormsö》则是纯器乐演奏，口簧琴、长笛与弦乐交织，营造出令人兴奋的失衡感。整张 EP 虽短，却已呈现一个成熟而有默契的乐队面貌，为后续全长专辑埋下伏笔。

items._cn_summary: 贝斯手兼作曲家Max Johnson发起了一项Kickstarter众筹计划，旨在发行五张录音作品，涵盖作曲与即兴音乐。这些项目包括与Anna Webber和Michael Sarin合作的全新三重奏作品，源自2022至2023年的巡演素材；以及与Nate Wooley、Brian等人合作的一套即兴再创作组曲，主题反思疫情期间停滞与疏离的状态。整体计划横跨当代即兴演奏与作曲领域，汇集多位纽约地下爵士与前卫音乐圈的活跃乐手。从目前披露的信息来看，五张专辑的发行模式本身具有实验意味——将巡演素材、反思性即兴与新作品并置，试图以多维度呈现一位贝斯手的创作全貌。然而由于原文仅为新闻式预告，缺乏实际音乐内容与听感描述，无法对其艺术成就做出具体判断。

items.body: Angus Batey revisits the history and lasting legacy of A Tribe Called Quest's Low End Theory There's a wonderful moment in Beats, Rhymes and Life: The Travels of A Tribe Called Quest, Michael Rapaport's fascinating documentary about A Tribe Called Quest. Jive records CEO Barry Weiss recalls the label's internal reaction when staff first heard the group's second LP, The Low End Theory. "It was very different to the first album," Weiss tells Rapaport. "It wasn't as 'left' in some ways, and we were concerned that maybe it was gonna miss the mark - that maybe they were trying to go too commercial, that it didn't have the artistic integrity that [the debut] People's Instinctive Travels [In the Paths of Rhythm]... The post 35 Years On: A Tribe Called Quest’s The Low End Theory Revisited appeared first on The Quietus.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦于A Tribe Called Quest的第二张专辑《The Low End Theory》35周年回顾。文章引用了厂牌CEO Barry Weiss的回忆，描述了Jive唱片内部最初的反应——担心这张专辑过于商业化，失去了首张专辑的实验性与艺术完整性。这一片段揭示了唱片工业对艺术性与商业性之间张力的敏感，同时也暗示了《The Low End Theory》实际上在两者之间找到了独特定位。文章内容为回顾性质的乐评切片，探讨了专辑的历史背景与持久影响，属于主流嘻哈/爵士说唱范畴，与用户偏好的实验前卫音乐有一定距离但存在跨界元素。

items.body: Boston gothic post-punk and deathrock band Gossip Collar has released “Eaten of Worms”, its third full-length album, on September 4, 2026 through Bat-Cave Productions. The ten-track record is available on CD and LP through the label, with a digital edition on Bandcamp. Eaten Of Worms by Gossip Collar ‘Eaten of Worms’ tracklist and credits Eaten of Worms was recorded and mixed by Marc Valois at Dead Moon Audio in Somerville, Massachusetts, and mastered by Jeff Lipton at Peerless Mastering in Boston. The album’s ten tracks are: Disguise My Heart Scavengers Big Top Comes Crashing Down Haerisis Dead Thing Why Me? Peaceful In Daylight Spelling Misery Unsafe State Merchants Of The Wave The record pairs electronic textures with serrated guitar work, running through recurring images of water, predatory animals and religious dread across its ten songs. CD and LP copies can be ordered directly through Bat-Cave Productions, with a download code included. About Gossip Collar Gossip Collar formed in Boston in the dark basement scene at the tail end of the pandemic, bringing together members previously involved with The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz and Secret Hearts. The band’s lineup is Victoria on vocals and guitar, Tom on guitar, Mark on bass and Megan on drums. Gossip Collar released a self-titled debut album on April 7, 2023, followed by spinning silk for parasites on October 31, 2024. Eaten of Worms, out September 4, 2026 via Bat-Cave Productions, is the band’s third album. Gossip Collar has performed alongside The March Violets, Pink Turns Blue, Rendez-Vous, Haunt Me, House of Harm, Fotocrime and Sympathy Flowers. Eaten of Worms extends that catalogue with the band’s most recent studio work to date. Follow Gossip Collar: – Bandcamp – Instagram

items.body: Berlin-based darkwave act Night Nail has released “Vile Train”, a gothic rock single that previews the band’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain, due November 6, 2026 through Icy Cold Records. The song arrives with an official video directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera. ‘Vile Train’ single details “Vile Train” was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. Frontman Brandon Robert said the track drew its initial inspiration from a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The video reunites the band with director Jean De Oliviera, whose previous work with Night Nail includes “Hollow Day,” “Little Armenia” and “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher.” Shot in black and white, it cuts between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor scenes set among stone arches and fountain basins. A full tracklist for Infinite Fountain has not been announced. The album also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the release with shows across the US, UK and Europe during 2026 and 2027. About Night Nail Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and relocated to Berlin in 2018, the same year the band’s debut album, LA Demons, appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed in 2020 through Cold Transmission, and Fates Explained arrived on Metropolis Records in 2023, mixed and mastered by Pete Burns of Kill Shelter; Side-Line covered the single “Fates Explained” at the time. The band followed with the archival release Early Demons and Demos and the remix album Fates Remade in 2024, after earlier singles including “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher” and “Cracks In My Heart”, the latter featuring Luna De La Torre on vocals. Night Nail’s catalogue connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes, a combination built up over four albums and multiple labels since the band’s Los Angeles beginnings. “Vile Train” and the forthcoming Infinite Fountain, out on Icy Cold Records, mark the band’s next chapter and its first full-length since 2023’s Fates Explained. Follow Night Nail: – Bandcamp – Spotify – Website

items._cn_summary: Night Nail 即将发行第四张录音室专辑《Infinite Fountain》，本文介绍其先行单曲《Vile Train》的相关信息。歌曲由 William Faith 在芝加哥 13 Studio 完成混音与后期制作，VV & the Void 贡献额外人声与吉他，灵感来自主唱 Brandon Robert 参观庞贝古城时所见一幅描绘天使与恶魔相拥的壁画，试图以扭曲而优美的方式呈现关于爱的暗黑真相。MV 由 Jean De Oliviera 执导，黑白影像在放大器场景与户外石拱、喷泉之间切换。乐队 2013 年于洛杉矶组建，2018 年迁至柏林，曾先后与 Cleopatra、Cold Transmission、Metropolis 等厂牌合作，将暗潮电子与哥特摇滚的情感张力相结合。本文为新闻通稿性质，未对音乐本身做深度评论，缺乏对声音设计、编曲或创新的具体分析，信息以厂牌背景与制作人员介绍为主。

items.body: You said we’d never change You said we’d never fall I held on to every word I believed it all Forever is an ambitious promise to make on behalf of two people who are still changing. Romance encourages this sort of confidence, giving even the most cautious among us the vocabulary of someone who has personally inspected the future. When the relationship ends, those assurances acquire a different meaning, and the person who believed them has to wonder how much of the deception they helped along. Leipzig’s Kalte Steine turns that uncomfortable recognition into the cool, deceptively buoyant synthpop of “Love Is A Lie.” Following the social suffocation explored in “Drowning,” the single brings the question of dishonesty into a more intimate setting, where two people discover that sincerity offers little protection against making promises they cannot keep. A breathy exclamation hangs in reverb as the title refrain begins, with cool synthesizer tones underneath. Bubbly figures and bell-like notes soon brighten the arrangement, joined by a danceable drum-machine beat whose straightforward momentum gives the song its immediate pop appeal. There is an easy catchiness to these parts, each phrase leaving enough room for the next to register. The declaration that love is a lie becomes remarkably easy to sing along with. Buzzing synths and guitar tones gather beneath the first verse, while a brief metallic ripple of programmed percussion adds a small disturbance to the steady beat. The vocal sits high in the register, smooth and quietly sorrowful, carrying disappointment through its tone as much as its words. Deep bass strumming adds weight below, grounding the brighter electronics in the song’s private reckoning. The arrangement keeps moving even as the singer returns to assurances that have become difficult to hear. Initially, the lyrics give that disappointment a familiar address: “You said we’d never change / You said we’d never fall.” Every promise belongs to someone else, and the singer occupies the apparently straightforward position of having trusted the wrong person. The repeated title sounds conclusive enough to close the case. Yet the second verse quietly changes the pronouns: “I said we’d never change / I said we’d never fall.” The same words now come from the person who has been condemning them, making the earlier accusation considerably harder to sustain. “I promised you forever / Like it could be true / Oh I believed it too” supplies the song’s most revealing admission. Both people have mistaken the intensity of a feeling for evidence that it will last. Desire makes the promise persuasive to the person speaking as well as the person listening, complicating the chorus’s sweeping verdict. Through the repeated “Promises,” the post-chorus keeps returning to that shared vocabulary, setting “Words of love / Hearts on fire” beside “A web of lies / Built on desire.” What once sounded reassuring has become a reminder of how willingly both participated. When the chorus returns, melodic guitar figures add detail without crowding the hook, their economical phrasing intricate enough to reward attention and direct enough to stick. A laser-like synth accent introduces a little electronic whimsy, suggesting the beginnings of acceptance within the song’s disappointment. That small, almost playful touch suits a lyric that has gradually surrendered its claim to innocence. By the end, “Love Is A Lie” sounds like something the singer is still trying to believe, perhaps because admitting that the love was real and the promises failed is harder. Listen to Love Is A Lie on Spotify below: Love Is A Lie continues the English-language direction heard on “Crying Out” and “Drowning,” extending a catalogue that also includes “Shattered,” “Dysthymia,” “Wüste aus Beton,” and “Kinder der Nacht.” As explored in our earlier feature on Kalte Steine, the project has moved between personal fracture, urban alienation, and nocturnal escape. Here, its attention settles on the distance between what lovers mean and what they can reasonably promise. Follow Kalte Steine: Instagram Spotify SoundCloud TikTok The post Leipzig Darkwave Project Kalte Steine Turns Broken Promises Into Bittersweet Synthpop on “Love Is A Lie” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._genre: synthpop / darkwave / post-punk
items._cn_summary: 莱比锡暗潮项目Kalte Steine在单曲《Love Is A Lie》中将破裂承诺化为略带忧伤的合成器流行。评论指出，歌曲以cool synthesizer tones与舞蹈化的鼓机节奏构成悦耳的合成器流行基底，呼吸感的人声在高音区游走，音色平滑而暗含失落。歌词叙事的精妙之处在于视角转换：首段主歌将矛头指向对方的不实承诺，副歌以"love is a lie"作出断言；然而第二段悄然将主语换为第一人称，承认自己也曾被欲望的说服力所蒙蔽，以为激情的强度等同于持久的保证。后副歌通过"Words of love"与"A web of lies"的并置，让原本安慰性的措辞转为对共同虚妄的提醒。合成器嗡鸣、深沉贝斯拨弦与金属质感打击乐层叠，使明亮电子音色与私密的情感清算并行不悖。

items._cn_summary: ExWHYZ的告别专辑《zION》汇集了80KIDZ、大泽伸一、电脑音乐俱乐部等创作者的作品，以精致的音色编织与深邃的旋律层次贯穿始终。KBSNK＋ISLTR的开篇曲目以细腻的音景建立空间感，随后合作的制作人们带来硬朗的舞曲节拍，形成强烈的张力对比。成员亲自作词的曲目在电子架构中展露内省的情感维度，而终曲以延展的氛围余韵收束全篇。作为解散前的最后作品，整张专辑在品质把控与概念统一上展现出成熟的创作意识，是一张高完成度的电子流行佳作。

items.album: John Coltrane 100: Soul Junction & First Meditations
items.excerpt: The Red Garland Quintet Featuring John Coltrane and Donald Byrd - Soul Junction (Prestige, 1960) Culinary writers frequently refer to comfort food. Soul Junction is my comfort music. items.body: The Red Garland Quintet Featuring John Coltrane and Donald Byrd - Soul Junction (Prestige, 1960) Culinary writers frequently refer to comfort food. Soul Junction is my comfort music. I go to this album when I’m not in the mood to be blown away by wild flights of improvised fury or complex compositions or arrangements. This is an “end of an exhausting day” or a “reminder that maybe all will be well” kind of an album. I love the relaxed, bluesy feel of it. Listen to Garland’s piano on the opening title track. It’s pure bliss. George Joyner’s bass is understated perfection. The piano trio portion of the track goes on so long and is so hypnotic that you’re to be forgiven if you forget there’s a sax and trumpet still to come. Hey, there’s the saxophone. It feels like Trane was digging Garland’s playing and was dying to join in. Recorded in 1957, Trane hadn’t perfected his style yet. But his genius is right there to hear. He’s fantastic on Dizzy’s classic Birk’s Works . Donald Byrd doesn’t get much mention on this website, but I love a lot of his Blue Note music. He’s the perfect trumpeter for this session. Garland wisely gives the two of them lots of space to play, and they take every advantage of it. John Coltrane- First Meditations (For Quartet) ( Impulse!, 1977) As far as I’m concerned, A Love Supreme is the greatest jazz album of all time and Coltrane’s classic quartet the greatest group. First Meditations (For Quartet) is a beautiful piece of music and a fascinating document of a band just on the verge of transforming, both in terms of its personnel and its approach to music. (I prefer to say “transforming” to “ending”.) The first track, Love, clearly recalls A Love Supreme, as if that classic album is the starting point of this new music. Trane is stunning as always and McCoy is the perfect accompanist. The best track, Joy, is relatively calm and peaceful, until it isn’t. It begins as any number of other tracks from this quartet and then Trane sits out. He’s let the remaining trio play some (for this group) fairly straightforward piano trio music. But then he returns with an absolute roar, as if he wants to break constraints the rest of us can’t see. This is one of several places you can see the seams of the band starting to tear. It’s fascinating to hear. Much of this music was reconsidered on the subsequent album Meditations with Trane’s new group. A comparison of the two albums and the approach of two different groups to the material is fascinating, the second album justifiably being the more renowned of the two. But I find the first to be the one I keep returning to, as if I don’t want to say goodbye to this quartet. I genuinely love this album, but I had an ulterior motive for writing about it here. It gives me the opportunity to tell the story of the time I met Elvin Jones. He had been doing a drum demonstration and a line formed afterwards for autograph seekers. When I arrived at the front of the line, I barely refrained from doing “We’re not worthy”, but I did tell him how much his music meant to me and said I’d be honored if he’d sign this album. He took the CD booklet from me, looked at it and asked “Did I play on this?”. (I assume that since the album wasn’t released until 10 years after it was recorded, he never saw the album cover.) I showed him his name in the booklet, he laughed and signed it, making this album all the more special to me. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评涉及两张专辑。《Soul Junction》来自Red Garland五重奏，录制于1957年，是一张硬波普风格的舒适型爵士作品，钢琴、蓝调和轻柔的萨克斯即兴交织，整体氛围放松，适合日常聆听，Coltrane尚未形成成熟风格，但天才已现端倪。《First Meditations (For Quartet)》是Coltrane经典四重奏向新方向过渡的重要录音，第一首Love呼应《A Love Supreme》，而Joy这首曲子先平静后爆发的结构，展示了乐队即将解体的内在张力。整篇评论是个人化的聆乐随笔，夹杂了作者偶遇Elvin Jones的经历，音乐分析与情感回忆相结合，文字温暖但缺乏深度学术视角。

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. Find the artist online. Sara Serpa - Encounters and Collisions (Review) Karine Polwart- Laws of Motion (Review) Live in the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, 2025

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑源自艺术家在爱丁堡皇家植物园的驻留项目，围绕园中最古老的一棵棕榈树展开叙事。声音设计家与作曲家Pippa Murphy参与制作，钢琴手Dave Milligan的伴奏克制而富有共鸣，整体以人声与钢琴为核心，加上精心编排的环境声景。专辑追溯这棵树的来源与历史，结尾揭示出两百年来人们对其物种身份的误认——原本以为是Sabal bermudana，实为Sabal mexicana，新的幼苗已在原地萌发。歌词与音乐中反复出现的短语形成记忆锚点，旋律带有苏格兰民谣的悲歌气质。乐评指出这张作品虽以简约编制呈现，却承载了关于自然、历史与传承的宏大主题，呈现出私密而庄严的双重质感。
